<script>
  // Restore the saved color scheme preference, or
  // enact the browser preference if "automatic", 
  // without expecting DOM load to have completed.
  //
  // Also restore any saved readingmode and ToC display preferences.
  function initializeReadingPreferences() {
    let saved_theme = localStorage.getItem("ar5iv_theme") || "automatic";
    if (saved_theme === "automatic") {
      if (window.matchMedia("(prefers-color-scheme: dark)").matches) {
        saved_theme = "dark";
      }
    }
    if (saved_theme == "dark") {
      document.documentElement.setAttribute("data-theme", "dark");
    } else {
      document.documentElement.setAttribute("data-theme", "light");
    }

    const tocDisplay = localStorage.getItem('arxiv_html_paper_toc_display');
    if (tocDisplay) {
      document.documentElement.setAttribute("data-toc-display", tocDisplay);
    }
    const readingMode = localStorage.getItem('arxiv_html_paper_reading_mode');
    if (readingMode) {
      document.documentElement.setAttribute("data-reading-mode", readingMode);
    }
    // Pre-apply spinout-banner dismissal here, before the banner paints, so it
    // never flashes in only to be hidden later by the deferred arxiv-header.js.
    // Key matches arxiv-header.js: "arxiv-banner-dismissed:" + data-banner-name.
    if (localStorage.getItem('arxiv-banner-dismissed:spinout-nonprofit')) {
      document.documentElement.setAttribute("data-banner-dismissed", "");
    }
  }
  // Run as soon as JS starts, to minimize repainting
  initializeReadingPreferences();
</script>

<article class="ltx_document">
<h1 class="ltx_title ltx_title_document">Communication-Efficient Personalized Adaptation

<br class="ltx_break">via Federated-Local Model Merging</h1>
<div class="ltx_authors">
<span class="ltx_creator ltx_role_author">
<span class="ltx_personname">Yinan Zou
</span><span class="ltx_author_notes"><span class="ltx_author_notes_content">
<span class="ltx_contact ltx_role_affiliation"><span class="ltx_contact_name">Affiliation: </span>Elmore Family School of Electrical and Computer Engineering, Purdue University
</span>
<span class="ltx_contact ltx_role_email"><span class="ltx_contact_name">Correspondence to: </span><a href="mailto:zou211@purdue.edu">zou211@purdue.edu</a>
</span></span></span></span>
<span class="ltx_author_before">  </span><span class="ltx_creator ltx_role_author">
<span class="ltx_personname">Md Kamran Chowdhury Shisher
</span><span class="ltx_author_notes"><span class="ltx_author_notes_content">
<span class="ltx_contact ltx_role_affiliation"><span class="ltx_contact_name">Affiliation: </span>Elmore Family School of Electrical and Computer Engineering, Purdue University
</span></span></span></span>
<span class="ltx_author_before">  </span><span class="ltx_creator ltx_role_author">
<span class="ltx_personname">Christopher G. Brinton
</span><span class="ltx_author_notes"><span class="ltx_author_notes_content">
<span class="ltx_contact ltx_role_affiliation"><span class="ltx_contact_name">Affiliation: </span>Elmore Family School of Electrical and Computer Engineering, Purdue University
</span></span></span></span>
<span class="ltx_author_before">  </span><span class="ltx_creator ltx_role_author">
<span class="ltx_personname">Vishrant Tripathi
</span><span class="ltx_author_notes"><span class="ltx_author_notes_content">
<span class="ltx_contact ltx_role_affiliation"><span class="ltx_contact_name">Affiliation: </span>Elmore Family School of Electrical and Computer Engineering, Purdue University
</span></span></span></span></div>

<div id="abstract1" class="ltx_abstract"><h6 class="ltx_title ltx_title_abstract">Abstract</h6>
    
<p id="abstract1.1" class="ltx_p">Parameter-efficient fine-tuning methods, such as LoRA, offer a practical way to adapt large vision and language models to client tasks. However, this becomes particularly challenging under task-level heterogeneity in federated deployments.
In this regime, personalization requires balancing <em id="abstract1.1.1" class="ltx_emph ltx_font_italic">general knowledge</em> with <em id="abstract1.1.2" class="ltx_emph ltx_font_italic">personalized knowledge</em>, yet existing approaches largely rely on heuristic mixing rules and lack theoretical justification. Moreover, prior model merging approaches are also computation and communication intensive, making the process inefficient in federated settings. In this work, we propose <span id="abstract1.1.3" class="ltx_text ltx_font_smallcaps">Potara</span>, a principled framework for federated personalization that constructs a personalized model for each client by merging two complementary models: (i) a federated model capturing <em id="abstract1.1.4" class="ltx_emph ltx_font_italic">general knowledge</em>, and (ii) a local model capturing <em id="abstract1.1.5" class="ltx_emph ltx_font_italic">personalized knowledge</em>. Through the construct of linear mode connectivity, we show that the expected task loss admits a variance trace upper bound, whose minimization yields closed-form optimal mixing weights that guarantee a tighter bound for the merged model than for either the federated or local model alone.
Experiments on vision and language benchmarks show that <span id="abstract1.1.6" class="ltx_text ltx_font_smallcaps">Potara</span> consistently improves personalization while reducing communication, leading to a strong performance-communication trade-off.</p>
  
</div>
<div class="ltx_keywords">
<h6 class="ltx_title ltx_title_keywords">Keywords: </h6>Machine Learning, ICML
</div>
<section id="S1" class="ltx_section">
<h2 class="ltx_title ltx_title_section"><span class="ltx_tag ltx_tag_section">1 </span>Introduction</h2>

<div id="S1.p1" class="ltx_para">
<p id="S1.p1.1" class="ltx_p">Large vision models (LVMs) and large language models (LLMs) have achieved remarkable progress, enabling their widespread adoption across diverse downstream applications <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_citep">(<a href="#bib.bib9" title="" class="ltx_ref">Zhao et al., 2023</a>; <a href="#bib.bib8" title="" class="ltx_ref">Awais et al., 2025</a>)</cite>.
Adapting pre-trained models to domain specific tasks typically requires fine-tuning on task relevant data, but full parameter fine-tuning is computationally expensive and impractical at scale.
To mitigate this cost, parameter-efficient fine-tuning methods have been developed, among which low-rank adaptation (LoRA) <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_citep">(<a href="#bib.bib52" title="" class="ltx_ref">Hu et al., 2022</a>)</cite> has become particularly popular.
Domain specific fine-tuning of large models often requires large heterogeneous datasets which are typically split across organizations and cannot be centralized due to privacy and security constraints.
Federated learning (FL) <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_citep">(<a href="#bib.bib36" title="" class="ltx_ref">McMahan et al., 2017</a>)</cite> addresses this issue by enabling collaborative training while keeping raw data local.</p>
</div>
<div id="S1.p2" class="ltx_para">
<p id="S1.p2.1" class="ltx_p">Federated large model fine-tuning <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_citep">(<a href="#bib.bib50" title="" class="ltx_ref">Zhang et al., 2024</a>)</cite> integrates FL with LoRA, allowing clients to update and communicate only LoRA modules while jointly learning a global model.
Despite its promise, federated LoRA fine-tuning faces pronounced <em id="S1.p2.1.1" class="ltx_emph ltx_font_italic">task heterogeneity</em>: different clients may pursue distinct, and sometimes even conflicting, objectives.
In such settings, the knowledge required by each client naturally decomposes into two complementary components:
(i) <em id="S1.p2.1.2" class="ltx_emph ltx_font_italic">general knowledge</em> that can be transferred across clients and tasks, and
(ii) <em id="S1.p2.1.3" class="ltx_emph ltx_font_italic">personalized knowledge</em> that is specific to each client’s local data and task.</p>
</div>
<div id="S1.p3" class="ltx_para">
<p id="S1.p3.1" class="ltx_p"><span id="S1.p3.1.1" class="ltx_text ltx_font_bold">Challenges.</span> A central challenge is how to balance cross-client <em id="S1.p3.1.2" class="ltx_emph ltx_font_italic">general knowledge</em> and client-specific <em id="S1.p3.1.3" class="ltx_emph ltx_font_italic">personalized knowledge</em>.
It remains unclear, from a principled theoretical perspective, how much emphasis should be placed on general versus personalized knowledge when forming the final client model.
Although recent methods attempt to provide a solution <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_citep">(<a href="#bib.bib48" title="" class="ltx_ref">Yang et al., 2024</a>; <a href="#bib.bib46" title="" class="ltx_ref">Bian et al., 2026</a>)</cite>, they lack theoretical justification, leaving a gap for theoretically-grounded solutions.
Additionally, communication is the primary bottleneck in FL, and LoRA-based training still requires the repeated transmission of parameters across many rounds.
These considerations call for an approach that (i) explicitly control the general-personalized trade-off in a principled manner and (ii) achieve favorable performance–communication trade-off in realistic federated deployments.</p>
</div>
<section id="S1.SS1" class="ltx_subsection">
<h3 class="ltx_title ltx_title_subsection"><span class="ltx_tag ltx_tag_subsection">1.1 </span>Contributions</h3>

<div id="S1.SS1.p1" class="ltx_para">
<p id="S1.SS1.p1.1" class="ltx_p">Motivated by these limitations, this work aims to develop a framework for efficient federated fine-tuning under task heterogeneity.
Our key contributions are as follows:</p>
<ul id="S1.I1" class="ltx_itemize">
<li id="S1.I1.i1" class="ltx_item" style="list-style-type:none;"><span class="ltx_tag ltx_tag_item">•</span> 
<div id="S1.I1.i1.p1" class="ltx_para">
<p id="S1.I1.i1.p1.1" class="ltx_p">We propose <span id="S1.I1.i1.p1.1.1" class="ltx_text ltx_font_smallcaps">Potara<span id="footnote1" class="ltx_note ltx_role_footnote"><sup class="ltx_note_mark">1</sup><span class="ltx_note_outer"><span class="ltx_note_content"><sup class="ltx_note_mark">1</sup>
                      <span class="ltx_tag ltx_tag_note"><span id="footnote1.1" class="ltx_text ltx_font_upright">1</span></span>
                      
                      
                      
                      
                      
                      
                      
                    <span id="footnote1.10" class="ltx_text">Potara</span><span id="footnote1.11" class="ltx_text ltx_font_upright"> derives its name from the Potara fusion in Dragon Ball, where two independent entities are merged into a single, and more powerful form.</span></span></span></span></span>, a federated LoRA personalization framework to jointly (i) achieve an effective trade-off between federation and personalization, and (ii) balance communication efficiency with performance.
<span id="S1.I1.i1.p1.1.2" class="ltx_text ltx_font_smallcaps">Potara</span> constructs a personalized model for each client by merging two complementary models: a collaborative federated model that captures <span id="S1.I1.i1.p1.1.3" class="ltx_text ltx_font_italic">general knowledge</span> across all clients, and a local fine-tuning model that emphasizes <span id="S1.I1.i1.p1.1.4" class="ltx_text ltx_font_italic">personalized knowledge</span>.</p>
</div></li>
<li id="S1.I1.i2" class="ltx_item" style="list-style-type:none;"><span class="ltx_tag ltx_tag_item">•</span> 
<div id="S1.I1.i2.p1" class="ltx_para">
<p id="S1.I1.i2.p1.1" class="ltx_p">To determine the mixing weight between the federated model and the local model, we develop a rigorous analysis grounded in linear mode connectivity (LMC).
We show that, within an LMC basin around the optimum, the expected excess task losses of the federated model, the local model, and their merged model admits an upper bound in which the key term is a variance trace (see Theorem <a href="#S3.Thmtheorem6" title="Theorem 3.6. ‣ 3.3 Determination of Mixing Weights ‣ 3 Our Method: Potara ‣ Communication-Efficient Personalized Adaptation via Federated-Local Model Merging" class="ltx_ref"><span class="ltx_text ltx_ref_tag">3.6</span></a>).
Minimizing this bound yields closed-form optimal mixing weights, which guarantee that the merged model achieves the tighter bound than both the federated model and the local model (see Lemma <a href="#S3.Thmtheorem7" title="Lemma 3.7. ‣ Proof sketch of Theorem . ‣ 3.3 Determination of Mixing Weights ‣ 3 Our Method: Potara ‣ Communication-Efficient Personalized Adaptation via Federated-Local Model Merging" class="ltx_ref"><span class="ltx_text ltx_ref_tag">3.7</span></a>).</p>
</div></li>
<li id="S1.I1.i3" class="ltx_item" style="list-style-type:none;"><span class="ltx_tag ltx_tag_item">•</span> 
<div id="S1.I1.i3.p1" class="ltx_para">
<p id="S1.I1.i3.p1.1" class="ltx_p">We conduct extensive experiments on vision and language benchmarks. The experimental results show that our method achieves superior performance compared to baseline methods while significantly reducing communication overhead, thereby offering a favorable performance-communication trade-off.</p>
</div></li>
</ul>
</div>
</section>
<section id="S1.SS2" class="ltx_subsection">
<h3 class="ltx_title ltx_title_subsection"><span class="ltx_tag ltx_tag_subsection">1.2 </span>Related Work</h3>

<div id="S1.SS2.p1" class="ltx_para">
<p id="S1.SS2.p1.1" class="ltx_p"><span id="S1.SS2.p1.1.1" class="ltx_text ltx_font_bold">Model Merging.</span>
Model merging aims to combine multiple task-specific models into a single model without additional training.
<cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_citet"><a href="#bib.bib22" title="" class="ltx_ref">Wortsman et al. (2022)</a></cite> utilized averaged parameters to construct the merged model.
To account for parameter importance, <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_citet"><a href="#bib.bib44" title="" class="ltx_ref">Matena and Raffel (2022)</a></cite> proposed weighted fusion, where merging weights are derived from the Fisher information matrix <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_citep">(<a href="#bib.bib33" title="" class="ltx_ref">Fisher, 1922</a>)</cite>.
<cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_citet"><a href="#bib.bib21" title="" class="ltx_ref">Jin et al. (2023)</a></cite> formulated model merging as a linear regression problem and obtained a closed-form solution.
Instead of averaging weights, <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_citet"><a href="#bib.bib47" title="" class="ltx_ref">Ilharco et al. (2023)</a></cite> introduced task vectors by subtracting the pre-trained parameters from each fine-tuned model, and then linearly combining these task vectors to form a merged model.
<cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_citet"><a href="#bib.bib20" title="" class="ltx_ref">Yadav et al. (2023)</a></cite> proposed to reduces conflicts in task vectors <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_citep">(<a href="#bib.bib47" title="" class="ltx_ref">Ilharco et al., 2023</a>)</cite> by trimming low-magnitude updates, resolving sign disagreements, and merging disjoint parameter subsets with consistent signs.
<cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_citet"><a href="#bib.bib19" title="" class="ltx_ref">Yu et al. (2024)</a></cite> further explored this issue by randomly dropping a subset of fine-tuned weights and rescaling the remainder, yielding sparse task vectors that alleviate destructive interference.
Most existing methods <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_citep">(<a href="#bib.bib47" title="" class="ltx_ref">Ilharco et al., 2023</a>; <a href="#bib.bib20" title="" class="ltx_ref">Yadav et al., 2023</a>; <a href="#bib.bib19" title="" class="ltx_ref">Yu et al., 2024</a>; <a href="#bib.bib2" title="" class="ltx_ref">Qi et al., 2025</a>; <a href="#bib.bib1" title="" class="ltx_ref">Stoica et al., 2025</a>)</cite> select merging weights via heuristic tuning (e.g., grid search), which is computation intensive.
In contrast, our approach derives the optimal mixing weights from theory, substantially improving efficiency by eliminating expensive per-client weight sweeps and repeated evaluations.</p>
</div>
<div id="S1.SS2.p2" class="ltx_para">
<p id="S1.SS2.p2.1" class="ltx_p"><span id="S1.SS2.p2.1.1" class="ltx_text ltx_font_bold">Personalized Federated Learning.</span> Personalized federated learning aims to overcome the limitation of a single global model by adapting client models to their local data distribution <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_citep">(<a href="#bib.bib17" title="" class="ltx_ref">Tan et al., 2022</a>)</cite>.
Common approaches include meta learning <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_citep">(<a href="#bib.bib31" title="" class="ltx_ref">Fallah et al., 2020</a>; <a href="#bib.bib16" title="" class="ltx_ref">Chen et al., 2018</a>)</cite>, partial model personalization <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_citep">(<a href="#bib.bib30" title="" class="ltx_ref">Collins et al., 2021</a>; <a href="#bib.bib18" title="" class="ltx_ref">Pillutla et al., 2022</a>)</cite>, multi-task learning <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_citep">(<a href="#bib.bib14" title="" class="ltx_ref">Smith et al., 2017</a>; <a href="#bib.bib13" title="" class="ltx_ref">Li et al., 2021</a>)</cite>, hypernetworks <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_citep">(<a href="#bib.bib15" title="" class="ltx_ref">Shamsian et al., 2021</a>)</cite>, and clustering <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_citep">(<a href="#bib.bib12" title="" class="ltx_ref">Duan et al., 2021</a>; <a href="#bib.bib11" title="" class="ltx_ref">Ghosh et al., 2020</a>)</cite>.
A related study on personalized FL and model merging, FedMerge <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_citep">(<a href="#bib.bib49" title="" class="ltx_ref">Chen et al., 2026</a>)</cite>, proposed a multi-model FL framework in which the server maintains a pool of global models, and each client obtains a personalized model by merging these server-side models.
However, the server stores multiple global models and perform gradient-based updates for each model in the pool, both the storage and computation overhead on the server scale linearly with the number of global models.
In contrast, our method follows a single-model paradigm where the server maintains only one global model and the server only needs to average the local models, making it substantially more resource efficient for large model fine-tuning.
Moreover, the above methods primarily address statistical heterogeneity (e.g., label distribution skew) and are typically evaluated on conventional small model architectures.
In contrast, we study a more realistic and challenging regime for large model adaptation, where heterogeneity manifests not only in label diversity but also in task diversity across clients.</p>
</div>
<div id="S1.SS2.p3" class="ltx_para">
<p id="S1.SS2.p3.1" class="ltx_p"><span id="S1.SS2.p3.1.1" class="ltx_text ltx_font_bold">Federated Fine-Tuning.</span> FedIT <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_citep">(<a href="#bib.bib50" title="" class="ltx_ref">Zhang et al., 2024</a>)</cite> integrated LoRA with FedAvg and is one of the earliest efforts to combine parameter-efficient adaptation with federated optimization.
Subsequent works studied federated LoRA under differential privacy <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_citep">(<a href="#bib.bib45" title="" class="ltx_ref">Sun et al., 2024</a>)</cite>, the asymmetric roles of LoRA matrices <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_citep">(<a href="#bib.bib51" title="" class="ltx_ref">Guo et al., 2025</a>)</cite>, and heterogeneous-rank LoRA matrices <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_citep">(<a href="#bib.bib53" title="" class="ltx_ref">Fang et al., 2025</a>; <a href="#bib.bib25" title="" class="ltx_ref">Cho et al., 2024</a>; <a href="#bib.bib24" title="" class="ltx_ref">Bai et al., 2024</a>; <a href="#bib.bib23" title="" class="ltx_ref">Wang et al., 2024</a>)</cite>.
<cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_citet"><a href="#bib.bib29" title="" class="ltx_ref">Hao et al. (2025)</a>; <a href="#bib.bib42" title="" class="ltx_ref">Qi et al. (2024)</a></cite> studied personalization under label-distribution heterogeneity while still assuming task-homogeneous adaptation.
Considering task heterogeneity, <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_citet"><a href="#bib.bib48" title="" class="ltx_ref">Yang et al. (2024)</a>; <a href="#bib.bib46" title="" class="ltx_ref">Bian et al. (2026)</a></cite> introduced global and local LoRA modules and combine them via a dynamic mixer.
Although empirically effective, such designs lack theoretical justification for determining the appropriate mixing weights between these two LoRA modules.
In contrast, our method derives the optimal mixing weight from a principled theoretical analysis.</p>
</div>
<figure id="alg1" class="ltx_float ltx_float_algorithm ltx_framed ltx_framed_top">
<figcaption class="ltx_caption"><span class="ltx_tag ltx_tag_float"><span id="alg1.3" class="ltx_text ltx_font_bold">Algorithm 1</span> </span> FedIT</figcaption>
<div id="alg1.4" class="ltx_listing ltx_framed ltx_framed_topbottom ltx_listing">
<div id="alg1.l1" class="ltx_listingline">
              <span class="ltx_tag ltx_tag_listingline"><span id="alg1.l1.1" class="ltx_text" style="font-size:80%;">1:</span></span>
              
              
             <span id="alg1.l1.3" class="ltx_text ltx_font_bold">Initialize</span>: Per-trained model <math id="alg1.l1.m1" class="ltx_Math" alttext="\mathbf{W}_{\mathrm{Pre}}" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><msub><mi>𝐖</mi><mi>Pre</mi></msub><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\mathbf{W}_{\mathrm{Pre}}</annotation></semantics></math>, initialized LoRA modules <math id="alg1.l1.m2" class="ltx_Math" alttext="\{\mathbf{B}^{0},\mathbf{A}^{0}\}" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><mo stretchy="false">{</mo><msup><mi>𝐁</mi><mn>0</mn></msup><mo>,</mo><msup><mi>𝐀</mi><mn>0</mn></msup><mo stretchy="false">}</mo></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\{\mathbf{B}^{0},\mathbf{A}^{0}\}</annotation></semantics></math>;

</div>
<div id="alg1.l2" class="ltx_listingline">
              <span class="ltx_tag ltx_tag_listingline"><span id="alg1.l2.1" class="ltx_text" style="font-size:80%;">2:</span></span>
              
              
             <span id="alg1.l2.3" class="ltx_text ltx_font_bold">for</span> communication round <math id="alg1.l2.m1" class="ltx_Math" alttext="t=0,1,\dots,T-1" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><mrow><mi>t</mi><mo>=</mo><mn>0</mn></mrow><mo>,</mo><mn>1</mn><mo>,</mo><mi mathvariant="normal">…</mi><mo>,</mo><mrow><mi>T</mi><mo>−</mo><mn>1</mn></mrow></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">t=0,1,\dots,T-1</annotation></semantics></math> <span id="alg1.l2.4" class="ltx_text ltx_font_bold">do</span>



</div>
<div id="alg1.l3" class="ltx_listingline">
              <span class="ltx_tag ltx_tag_listingline"><span id="alg1.l3.1" class="ltx_text" style="font-size:80%;">3:</span></span>
              
              
              Server broadcasts the current global LoRA modules <math id="alg1.l3.m1" class="ltx_Math" alttext="\{\mathbf{B}^{t},\mathbf{A}^{t}\}" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><mo stretchy="false">{</mo><msup><mi>𝐁</mi><mi>t</mi></msup><mo>,</mo><msup><mi>𝐀</mi><mi>t</mi></msup><mo stretchy="false">}</mo></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\{\mathbf{B}^{t},\mathbf{A}^{t}\}</annotation></semantics></math> to all clients.

</div>
<div id="alg1.l4" class="ltx_listingline">
              <span class="ltx_tag ltx_tag_listingline"><span id="alg1.l4.1" class="ltx_text" style="font-size:80%;">4:</span></span>
              
              
              <span id="alg1.l4.3" class="ltx_text ltx_font_bold">for</span> each client <math id="alg1.l4.m1" class="ltx_Math" alttext="i=1,\dots,N" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><mrow><mi>i</mi><mo>=</mo><mn>1</mn></mrow><mo>,</mo><mi mathvariant="normal">…</mi><mo>,</mo><mi>N</mi></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">i=1,\dots,N</annotation></semantics></math> in parallel <span id="alg1.l4.4" class="ltx_text ltx_font_bold">do</span>



</div>
<div id="alg1.l5" class="ltx_listingline">
              <span class="ltx_tag ltx_tag_listingline"><span id="alg1.l5.1" class="ltx_text" style="font-size:80%;">5:</span></span>
              
              
               Client <math id="alg1.l5.m1" class="ltx_Math" alttext="i" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mi>i</mi><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">i</annotation></semantics></math> keeps pre-trained model <math id="alg1.l5.m2" class="ltx_Math" alttext="\mathbf{W}_{\mathrm{Pre}}" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><msub><mi>𝐖</mi><mi>Pre</mi></msub><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\mathbf{W}_{\mathrm{Pre}}</annotation></semantics></math> frozen and updates only LoRA modules to obtain <math id="alg1.l5.m3" class="ltx_Math" alttext="\{\mathbf{B}^{(i),t},\mathbf{A}^{(i),t}\}" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><mo stretchy="false">{</mo><msup><mi>𝐁</mi><mrow><mrow><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mi>i</mi><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></mrow><mo>,</mo><mi>t</mi></mrow></msup><mo>,</mo><msup><mi>𝐀</mi><mrow><mrow><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mi>i</mi><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></mrow><mo>,</mo><mi>t</mi></mrow></msup><mo stretchy="false">}</mo></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\{\mathbf{B}^{(i),t},\mathbf{A}^{(i),t}\}</annotation></semantics></math>.

</div>
<div id="alg1.l6" class="ltx_listingline">
              <span class="ltx_tag ltx_tag_listingline"><span id="alg1.l6.1" class="ltx_text" style="font-size:80%;">6:</span></span>
              
              
               Client <math id="alg1.l6.m1" class="ltx_Math" alttext="i" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mi>i</mi><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">i</annotation></semantics></math> uploads its local LoRA modules <math id="alg1.l6.m2" class="ltx_Math" alttext="\{\mathbf{B}^{(i),t},\mathbf{A}^{(i),t}\}" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><mo stretchy="false">{</mo><msup><mi>𝐁</mi><mrow><mrow><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mi>i</mi><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></mrow><mo>,</mo><mi>t</mi></mrow></msup><mo>,</mo><msup><mi>𝐀</mi><mrow><mrow><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mi>i</mi><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></mrow><mo>,</mo><mi>t</mi></mrow></msup><mo stretchy="false">}</mo></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\{\mathbf{B}^{(i),t},\mathbf{A}^{(i),t}\}</annotation></semantics></math> to the server.

</div>
<div id="alg1.l7" class="ltx_listingline">
              <span class="ltx_tag ltx_tag_listingline"><span id="alg1.l7.1" class="ltx_text" style="font-size:80%;">7:</span></span>
              
              
              <span id="alg1.l7.3" class="ltx_text ltx_font_bold">end</span> <span id="alg1.l7.4" class="ltx_text ltx_font_bold">for</span>
</div>
<div id="alg1.l8" class="ltx_listingline">
              <span class="ltx_tag ltx_tag_listingline"><span id="alg1.l8.1" class="ltx_text" style="font-size:80%;">8:</span></span>
              
              
              Server updates the global LoRA modules via

</section>
<section id="S2" class="ltx_section">
<h2 class="ltx_title ltx_title_section"><span class="ltx_tag ltx_tag_section">2 </span>Preliminaries and Notation</h2>

<div id="S2.p1" class="ltx_para">
<p id="S2.p1.1" class="ltx_p">In this section, we introduce the preliminary concepts and notation used throughout the paper, including LoRA, federated fine-tuning, and linear mode connectivity.</p>
</div>
<section id="S2.SS1" class="ltx_subsection">
<h3 class="ltx_title ltx_title_subsection"><span class="ltx_tag ltx_tag_subsection">2.1 </span>Parameter-Efficient Fine-Tuning: LoRA</h3>

<div id="S2.SS1.p1" class="ltx_para">
<p id="S2.SS1.p1.1" class="ltx_p">Consider a pre-trained model with parameters <math id="S2.SS1.p1.m1" class="ltx_Math" alttext="\mathbf{W}_{\mathrm{Pre}}\in\mathbb{R}^{m\times n}" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><msub><mi>𝐖</mi><mi>Pre</mi></msub><mo>∈</mo><msup><mi>ℝ</mi><mrow><mi>m</mi><mo lspace="0.222em" rspace="0.222em">×</mo><mi>n</mi></mrow></msup></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\mathbf{W}_{\mathrm{Pre}}\in\mathbb{R}^{m\times n}</annotation></semantics></math>.
We denote
<math id="S2.SS1.p1.m2" class="ltx_Math" alttext="\Delta\mathbf{W}\in\mathbb{R}^{m\times n}" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><mrow><mi mathvariant="normal">Δ</mi><mo lspace="0em" rspace="0em">​</mo><mi>𝐖</mi></mrow><mo>∈</mo><msup><mi>ℝ</mi><mrow><mi>m</mi><mo lspace="0.222em" rspace="0.222em">×</mo><mi>n</mi></mrow></msup></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\Delta\mathbf{W}\in\mathbb{R}^{m\times n}</annotation></semantics></math> as the trainable update matrix during fine-tuning.
Instead of updating all parameters in <math id="S2.SS1.p1.m3" class="ltx_Math" alttext="\Delta\mathbf{W}" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><mi mathvariant="normal">Δ</mi><mo lspace="0em" rspace="0em">​</mo><mi>𝐖</mi></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\Delta\mathbf{W}</annotation></semantics></math>, LoRA <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_citep">(<a href="#bib.bib52" title="" class="ltx_ref">Hu et al., 2022</a>)</cite> decomposes
<math id="S2.SS1.p1.m4" class="ltx_Math" alttext="\Delta\mathbf{W}" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><mi mathvariant="normal">Δ</mi><mo lspace="0em" rspace="0em">​</mo><mi>𝐖</mi></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\Delta\mathbf{W}</annotation></semantics></math> into two low-rank matrices
<math id="S2.SS1.p1.m5" class="ltx_Math" alttext="\mathbf{A}\in\mathbb{R}^{r\times n}" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><mi>𝐀</mi><mo>∈</mo><msup><mi>ℝ</mi><mrow><mi>r</mi><mo lspace="0.222em" rspace="0.222em">×</mo><mi>n</mi></mrow></msup></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\mathbf{A}\in\mathbb{R}^{r\times n}</annotation></semantics></math> and <math id="S2.SS1.p1.m6" class="ltx_Math" alttext="\mathbf{B}\in\mathbb{R}^{m\times r}" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><mi>𝐁</mi><mo>∈</mo><msup><mi>ℝ</mi><mrow><mi>m</mi><mo lspace="0.222em" rspace="0.222em">×</mo><mi>r</mi></mrow></msup></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\mathbf{B}\in\mathbb{R}^{m\times r}</annotation></semantics></math>,
where <math id="S2.SS1.p1.m7" class="ltx_Math" alttext="r\ll\min(m,n)" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><mi>r</mi><mo>≪</mo><mrow><mi>min</mi><mo>⁡</mo><mrow><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mi>m</mi><mo>,</mo><mi>n</mi><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></mrow></mrow></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">r\ll\min(m,n)</annotation></semantics></math>. This decomposition allows the fine-tuning to focus on the
significantly smaller low-rank matrices <math id="S2.SS1.p1.m8" class="ltx_Math" alttext="\mathbf{A}" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mi>𝐀</mi><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\mathbf{A}</annotation></semantics></math> and <math id="S2.SS1.p1.m9" class="ltx_Math" alttext="\mathbf{B}" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mi>𝐁</mi><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\mathbf{B}</annotation></semantics></math> instead of the full
matrix <math id="S2.SS1.p1.m10" class="ltx_Math" alttext="\Delta\mathbf{W}" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><mi mathvariant="normal">Δ</mi><mo lspace="0em" rspace="0em">​</mo><mi>𝐖</mi></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\Delta\mathbf{W}</annotation></semantics></math>.
Consequently, the total number of trainable parameters is reduced
from <math id="S2.SS1.p1.m11" class="ltx_Math" alttext="m\times n" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><mi>m</mi><mo lspace="0.222em" rspace="0.222em">×</mo><mi>n</mi></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">m\times n</annotation></semantics></math> to <math id="S2.SS1.p1.m12" class="ltx_Math" alttext="r\times(m+n)" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><mi>r</mi><mo lspace="0.222em" rspace="0.222em">×</mo><mrow><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mrow><mi>m</mi><mo>+</mo><mi>n</mi></mrow><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></mrow></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">r\times(m+n)</annotation></semantics></math>. The model parameters after fine-tuning are given by:</p>
<table id="S2.EGx1" class="ltx_equationgroup ltx_eqn_align ltx_eqn_table">

<tbody id="S2.E1"><tr class="ltx_equation ltx_eqn_row ltx_align_baseline">
<td class="ltx_eqn_cell ltx_eqn_center_padleft"></td>
<td class="ltx_td ltx_align_right ltx_eqn_cell"><math id="S2.E1.m1" class="ltx_Math" alttext="\displaystyle\mathbf{W}_{\mathrm{FT}}=\mathbf{W}_{\mathrm{Pre}}+\Delta\mathbf{W}=\mathbf{W}_{\mathrm{Pre}}+\mathbf{B}\mathbf{A}," display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><mrow><msub><mi>𝐖</mi><mi>FT</mi></msub><mo>=</mo><mrow><msub><mi>𝐖</mi><mi>Pre</mi></msub><mo>+</mo><mrow><mi mathvariant="normal">Δ</mi><mo lspace="0em" rspace="0em">​</mo><mi>𝐖</mi></mrow></mrow><mo>=</mo><mrow><msub><mi>𝐖</mi><mi>Pre</mi></msub><mo>+</mo><mi>𝐁𝐀</mi></mrow></mrow><mo>,</mo></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\displaystyle\mathbf{W}_{\mathrm{FT}}=\mathbf{W}_{\mathrm{Pre}}+\Delta\mathbf{W}=\mathbf{W}_{\mathrm{Pre}}+\mathbf{B}\mathbf{A},</annotation></semantics></math></td>
<td class="ltx_eqn_cell ltx_eqn_center_padright"></td>
<td rowspan="1" class="ltx_eqn_cell ltx_eqn_eqno ltx_align_middle ltx_align_right"><span class="ltx_tag ltx_tag_equation ltx_align_right">(1)</span></td></tr></tbody>
</table>
<p id="S2.SS1.p1.2" class="ltx_p">where <math id="S2.SS1.p1.m13" class="ltx_Math" alttext="\mathbf{A}" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mi>𝐀</mi><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\mathbf{A}</annotation></semantics></math> is typically initialized with random Gaussian values and <math id="S2.SS1.p1.m14" class="ltx_Math" alttext="\mathbf{B}" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mi>𝐁</mi><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\mathbf{B}</annotation></semantics></math> is initialized to zero <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_citep">(<a href="#bib.bib52" title="" class="ltx_ref">Hu et al., 2022</a>; <a href="#bib.bib7" title="" class="ltx_ref">Hayou et al., 2024</a>)</cite>.</p>
</div>
</section>
<section id="S2.SS2" class="ltx_subsection">
<h3 class="ltx_title ltx_title_subsection"><span class="ltx_tag ltx_tag_subsection">2.2 </span>Federated LoRA Fine-Tuning</h3>

<div id="S2.SS2.p1" class="ltx_para">
<p id="S2.SS2.p1.1" class="ltx_p">FedIT <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_citep">(<a href="#bib.bib50" title="" class="ltx_ref">Zhang et al., 2024</a>)</cite> integrates LoRA <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_citep">(<a href="#bib.bib52" title="" class="ltx_ref">Hu et al., 2022</a>)</cite> with the FedAvg <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_citep">(<a href="#bib.bib36" title="" class="ltx_ref">McMahan et al., 2017</a>)</cite> framework.
The procedure of FedIT is summarized in Algorithm <a href="#alg1" title="Algorithm 1 ‣ 1.2 Related Work ‣ 1 Introduction ‣ Communication-Efficient Personalized Adaptation via Federated-Local Model Merging" class="ltx_ref"><span class="ltx_text ltx_ref_tag">1</span></a>.
FedIT aims to minimize a global loss function subject to the consensus constraints <math id="S2.SS2.p1.m1" class="ltx_Math" alttext="{\bf B}^{(1)}=\ldots={\bf B}^{(N)}" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><msup><mi>𝐁</mi><mrow><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mn>1</mn><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></mrow></msup><mo>=</mo><mi mathvariant="normal">…</mi><mo>=</mo><msup><mi>𝐁</mi><mrow><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mi>N</mi><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></mrow></msup></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">{\bf B}^{(1)}=\ldots={\bf B}^{(N)}</annotation></semantics></math> and <math id="S2.SS2.p1.m2" class="ltx_Math" alttext="{\bf A}^{(1)}=\ldots={\bf A}^{(N)}" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><msup><mi>𝐀</mi><mrow><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mn>1</mn><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></mrow></msup><mo>=</mo><mi mathvariant="normal">…</mi><mo>=</mo><msup><mi>𝐀</mi><mrow><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mi>N</mi><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></mrow></msup></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">{\bf A}^{(1)}=\ldots={\bf A}^{(N)}</annotation></semantics></math> where <math id="S2.SS2.p1.m3" class="ltx_Math" alttext="{\bf B}^{(i)}" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><msup><mi>𝐁</mi><mrow><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mi>i</mi><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></mrow></msup><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">{\bf B}^{(i)}</annotation></semantics></math> and <math id="S2.SS2.p1.m4" class="ltx_Math" alttext="{\bf A}^{(i)}" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><msup><mi>𝐀</mi><mrow><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mi>i</mi><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></mrow></msup><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">{\bf A}^{(i)}</annotation></semantics></math> denotes the LoRA matrices at client <math id="S2.SS2.p1.m5" class="ltx_Math" alttext="i" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mi>i</mi><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">i</annotation></semantics></math>.
Consequently, it ultimately yields a single model shared across all clients.</p>
</div>
</section>
<section id="S2.SS3" class="ltx_subsection">
<h3 class="ltx_title ltx_title_subsection"><span class="ltx_tag ltx_tag_subsection">2.3 </span>Linear Mode Connectivity</h3>

<div id="S2.SS3.p1" class="ltx_para">
<p id="S2.SS3.p1.1" class="ltx_p">Prior works <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_citep">(<a href="#bib.bib39" title="" class="ltx_ref">Draxler et al., 2018</a>; <a href="#bib.bib41" title="" class="ltx_ref">Garipov et al., 2018</a>)</cite> show that the minima found by two independently trained neural networks can be connected by a simple path along which the loss or accuracy remains nearly constant.
This phenomenon is referred to as mode connectivity.
Subsequent studies <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_citep">(<a href="#bib.bib38" title="" class="ltx_ref">Nagarajan and Kolter, 2019</a>; <a href="#bib.bib40" title="" class="ltx_ref">Frankle et al., 2020</a>)</cite> further show that when neural networks are trained from the same initialization, the resulting well-trained models can be connected by a linear path, known as linear mode connectivity (LMC).
We restate the definition of LMC used in <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_citep">(<a href="#bib.bib40" title="" class="ltx_ref">Frankle et al., 2020</a>; <a href="#bib.bib6" title="" class="ltx_ref">Zhou et al., 2023</a>)</cite>.</p>
</div>
<div id="S2.Thmtheorem1" class="ltx_theorem ltx_theorem_definition">
<h6 class="ltx_title ltx_runin ltx_title_theorem"><span class="ltx_tag ltx_tag_theorem"><span id="S2.Thmtheorem1.2" class="ltx_text ltx_font_bold">Definition 2.1</span></span><span id="S2.Thmtheorem1.3" class="ltx_text ltx_font_bold">.</span></h6>
<div id="S2.Thmtheorem1.p1" class="ltx_para">
<p id="S2.Thmtheorem1.p1.1" class="ltx_p"><cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_citep">(<a href="#bib.bib40" title="" class="ltx_ref">Frankle et al., 2020</a>; <a href="#bib.bib6" title="" class="ltx_ref">Zhou et al., 2023</a>)</cite>
Given a dataset <math id="S2.Thmtheorem1.p1.m1" class="ltx_Math" alttext="\mathcal{D}" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mi class="ltx_font_mathcaligraphic">𝒟</mi><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\mathcal{D}</annotation></semantics></math> and two well-trained models <math id="S2.Thmtheorem1.p1.m2" class="ltx_Math" alttext="\mathbf{W}_{1}" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><msub><mi>𝐖</mi><mn>1</mn></msub><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\mathbf{W}_{1}</annotation></semantics></math> and <math id="S2.Thmtheorem1.p1.m3" class="ltx_Math" alttext="\mathbf{W}_{2}" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><msub><mi>𝐖</mi><mn>2</mn></msub><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\mathbf{W}_{2}</annotation></semantics></math> such that
<math id="S2.Thmtheorem1.p1.m4" class="ltx_Math" alttext="f(\mathbf{W}_{1};\mathcal{D})\approx f(\mathbf{W}_{2};\mathcal{D})" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><mrow><mi>f</mi><mo>⁡</mo><mrow><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><msub><mi>𝐖</mi><mn>1</mn></msub><mo>,</mo><mi class="ltx_font_mathcaligraphic">𝒟</mi><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></mrow></mrow><mo>≈</mo><mrow><mi>f</mi><mo>⁡</mo><mrow><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><msub><mi>𝐖</mi><mn>2</mn></msub><mo>,</mo><mi class="ltx_font_mathcaligraphic">𝒟</mi><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></mrow></mrow></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">f(\mathbf{W}_{1};\mathcal{D})\approx f(\mathbf{W}_{2};\mathcal{D})</annotation></semantics></math>,
we say that <math id="S2.Thmtheorem1.p1.m5" class="ltx_Math" alttext="\mathbf{W}_{1}" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><msub><mi>𝐖</mi><mn>1</mn></msub><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\mathbf{W}_{1}</annotation></semantics></math> and <math id="S2.Thmtheorem1.p1.m6" class="ltx_Math" alttext="\mathbf{W}_{2}" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><msub><mi>𝐖</mi><mn>2</mn></msub><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\mathbf{W}_{2}</annotation></semantics></math> are linearly connected if they satisfy</p>
<table id="S2.EGx2" class="ltx_equationgroup ltx_eqn_align ltx_eqn_table">

<tbody id="S2.Ex2"><tr class="ltx_equation ltx_eqn_row ltx_align_baseline">
<td class="ltx_eqn_cell ltx_eqn_center_padleft"></td>
<td class="ltx_td ltx_eqn_cell"></td>
<td class="ltx_td ltx_align_left ltx_eqn_cell"><math id="S2.Ex2.m1" class="ltx_Math" alttext="\displaystyle f(\lambda_{1}\mathbf{W}_{1}+\lambda_{2}\mathbf{W}_{2};\mathcal{D})\approx f(\mathbf{W}_{1};\mathcal{D})," display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><mrow><mrow><mi>f</mi><mo>⁡</mo><mrow><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mrow><mrow><msub><mi>λ</mi><mn>1</mn></msub><mo lspace="0em" rspace="0em">​</mo><msub><mi>𝐖</mi><mn>1</mn></msub></mrow><mo>+</mo><mrow><msub><mi>λ</mi><mn>2</mn></msub><mo lspace="0em" rspace="0em">​</mo><msub><mi>𝐖</mi><mn>2</mn></msub></mrow></mrow><mo>,</mo><mi class="ltx_font_mathcaligraphic">𝒟</mi><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></mrow></mrow><mo>≈</mo><mrow><mi>f</mi><mo>⁡</mo><mrow><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><msub><mi>𝐖</mi><mn>1</mn></msub><mo>,</mo><mi class="ltx_font_mathcaligraphic">𝒟</mi><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></mrow></mrow></mrow><mo>,</mo></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\displaystyle f(\lambda_{1}\mathbf{W}_{1}+\lambda_{2}\mathbf{W}_{2};\mathcal{D})\approx f(\mathbf{W}_{1};\mathcal{D}),</annotation></semantics></math></td>
<td class="ltx_eqn_cell ltx_eqn_center_padright"></td></tr></tbody>
<tbody id="S2.E2"><tr class="ltx_equation ltx_eqn_row ltx_align_baseline">
<td class="ltx_eqn_cell ltx_eqn_center_padleft"></td>
<td class="ltx_td ltx_eqn_cell"></td>
<td class="ltx_td ltx_align_left ltx_eqn_cell"><math id="S2.E2.m1" class="ltx_Math" alttext="\displaystyle\quad\quad\quad\quad\quad\quad\quad\,\forall\,\lambda_{1},\lambda_{2}\geq 0,\,\lambda_{1}+\lambda_{2}=1," display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><mrow><mrow><mrow><mrow><mo rspace="0.337em">∀</mo><msub><mi>λ</mi><mn>1</mn></msub></mrow><mo>,</mo><msub><mi>λ</mi><mn>2</mn></msub></mrow><mo>≥</mo><mn>0</mn></mrow><mo rspace="0.337em">,</mo><mrow><mrow><msub><mi>λ</mi><mn>1</mn></msub><mo>+</mo><msub><mi>λ</mi><mn>2</mn></msub></mrow><mo>=</mo><mn>1</mn></mrow></mrow><mo>,</mo></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\displaystyle\quad\quad\quad\quad\quad\quad\quad\,\forall\,\lambda_{1},\lambda_{2}\geq 0,\,\lambda_{1}+\lambda_{2}=1,</annotation></semantics></math></td>
<td class="ltx_eqn_cell ltx_eqn_center_padright"></td>
<td rowspan="1" class="ltx_eqn_cell ltx_eqn_eqno ltx_align_middle ltx_align_right"><span class="ltx_tag ltx_tag_equation ltx_align_right">(2)</span></td></tr></tbody>
</table>
<p id="S2.Thmtheorem1.p1.2" class="ltx_p">where <math id="S2.Thmtheorem1.p1.m7" class="ltx_Math" alttext="f(\mathbf{W};\mathcal{D})" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><mi>f</mi><mo>⁡</mo><mrow><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mi>𝐖</mi><mo>,</mo><mi class="ltx_font_mathcaligraphic">𝒟</mi><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></mrow></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">f(\mathbf{W};\mathcal{D})</annotation></semantics></math> denotes the loss of model <math id="S2.Thmtheorem1.p1.m8" class="ltx_Math" alttext="\mathbf{W}" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mi>𝐖</mi><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\mathbf{W}</annotation></semantics></math> on dataset <math id="S2.Thmtheorem1.p1.m9" class="ltx_Math" alttext="\mathcal{D}" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mi class="ltx_font_mathcaligraphic">𝒟</mi><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\mathcal{D}</annotation></semantics></math>.</p>
</div>
</div>
<div id="S2.SS3.p2" class="ltx_para">
<p id="S2.SS3.p2.1" class="ltx_p">In Definition <a href="#S2.Thmtheorem1" title="Definition 2.1. ‣ 2.3 Linear Mode Connectivity ‣ 2 Preliminaries and Notation ‣ Communication-Efficient Personalized Adaptation via Federated-Local Model Merging" class="ltx_ref"><span class="ltx_text ltx_ref_tag">2.1</span></a>, two models <math id="S2.SS3.p2.m1" class="ltx_Math" alttext="\mathbf{W}_{1}" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><msub><mi>𝐖</mi><mn>1</mn></msub><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\mathbf{W}_{1}</annotation></semantics></math> and <math id="S2.SS3.p2.m2" class="ltx_Math" alttext="\mathbf{W}_{2}" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><msub><mi>𝐖</mi><mn>2</mn></msub><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\mathbf{W}_{2}</annotation></semantics></math> are linearly connected if the loss of the interpolated mode remains nearly unchanged.
In other words, <math id="S2.SS3.p2.m3" class="ltx_Math" alttext="\mathbf{W}_{1}" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><msub><mi>𝐖</mi><mn>1</mn></msub><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\mathbf{W}_{1}</annotation></semantics></math> and <math id="S2.SS3.p2.m4" class="ltx_Math" alttext="\mathbf{W}_{2}" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><msub><mi>𝐖</mi><mn>2</mn></msub><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\mathbf{W}_{2}</annotation></semantics></math> lie within the same flat basin of the loss landscape, and their linear interpolation remains inside this basin <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_citep">(<a href="#bib.bib37" title="" class="ltx_ref">Neyshabur et al., 2020</a>)</cite>.</p>
</div>
<figure id="S2.F1" class="ltx_figure"><img src="2602.18658v1/method2.png" id="S2.F1.g1" class="ltx_graphics ltx_centering ltx_img_landscape" style="aspect-ratio:471/246;" width="471" height="246" alt="Refer to caption">
<figcaption class="ltx_caption ltx_centering"><span class="ltx_tag ltx_tag_figure"><span id="S2.F1.4" class="ltx_text" style="font-size:90%;">Figure 1</span>: </span><span id="S2.F1.5" class="ltx_text" style="font-size:90%;">Illustration of <span id="S2.F1.5.1" class="ltx_text ltx_font_smallcaps">Potara</span>.
We train a FedIT model via FL and train local fine-tuning models.
We obtain the final personalized model by weighted merging these FedIT and local models.</span></figcaption>
</figure>
</section>
</section>
<section id="S3" class="ltx_section">
<h2 class="ltx_title ltx_title_section"><span class="ltx_tag ltx_tag_section">3 </span>Our Method: <span id="S3.2" class="ltx_text ltx_font_smallcaps">Potara</span></h2>

<div id="S3.p1" class="ltx_para">
<p id="S3.p1.1" class="ltx_p">In this section, we propose <span id="S3.p1.1.1" class="ltx_text ltx_font_smallcaps">Potara</span>, which achieves a principled trade-off between federation and personalization while simultaneously balancing communication efficiency and performance.</p>
</div>
<section id="S3.SS1" class="ltx_subsection">
<h3 class="ltx_title ltx_title_subsection"><span class="ltx_tag ltx_tag_subsection">3.1 </span>Motivation</h3>

<div id="S3.SS1.p1" class="ltx_para">
<p id="S3.SS1.p1.1" class="ltx_p">In large model fine-tuning, different clients usually hold data from distinct tasks (e.g., question classification versus sentiment analysis) <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_citep">(<a href="#bib.bib31" title="" class="ltx_ref">Fallah et al., 2020</a>; <a href="#bib.bib30" title="" class="ltx_ref">Collins et al., 2021</a>; <a href="#bib.bib46" title="" class="ltx_ref">Bian et al., 2026</a>; <a href="#bib.bib48" title="" class="ltx_ref">Yang et al., 2024</a>; <a href="#bib.bib32" title="" class="ltx_ref">Tian et al., 2023</a>)</cite>.
In such task-heterogeneous settings, consensus-based FL methods often underperform, since enforcing a single shared solution neglects both task diversity and the need for client-specific adaptation.
A trivial alternative is to let each client fine-tune independently without communication.
However, the number of local data samples is typically insufficient to train a satisfactory model in practical settings.
By exchanging information across clients, each client can exploit transferable knowledge learned elsewhere to improve its own model.
Accordingly, personalized federated fine-tuning aims to learn a client-specific model that effectively combines <em id="S3.SS1.p1.1.1" class="ltx_emph ltx_font_italic">general knowledge</em> across clients with <em id="S3.SS1.p1.1.2" class="ltx_emph ltx_font_italic">personalized knowledge</em> adapted to the client’s local task.</p>
</div>
</section>
<section id="S3.SS2" class="ltx_subsection">
<h3 class="ltx_title ltx_title_subsection"><span class="ltx_tag ltx_tag_subsection">3.2 </span>Federated-Local Model Merging</h3>

<div id="S3.SS2.p1" class="ltx_para">
<p id="S3.SS2.p1.1" class="ltx_p">Model merging provides a lightweight mechanism for combining complementary capabilities from multiple fine-tuned models without additional joint training.
Building on this idea, we propose <span id="S3.SS2.p1.1.1" class="ltx_text ltx_font_smallcaps">Potara</span>, which constructs a personalized model for each client by merging two complementary models:</p>
<ul id="S3.I1" class="ltx_itemize">
<li id="S3.I1.i1" class="ltx_item" style="list-style-type:none;"><span class="ltx_tag ltx_tag_item">•</span> 
<div id="S3.I1.i1.p1" class="ltx_para">
<p id="S3.I1.i1.p1.1" class="ltx_p">a collaborative FedIT model learned through cross-client communication,</p>
</div></li>
<li id="S3.I1.i2" class="ltx_item" style="list-style-type:none;"><span class="ltx_tag ltx_tag_item">•</span> 
<div id="S3.I1.i2.p1" class="ltx_para">
<p id="S3.I1.i2.p1.1" class="ltx_p">a purely local model fine-tuned only on that client's data.</p>
</div></li>
</ul>
<p id="S3.SS2.p1.2" class="ltx_p">Intuitively, the FedIT model captures <em id="S3.SS2.p1.2.1" class="ltx_emph ltx_font_italic">general knowledge</em> distilled from all clients.
In contrast, the local model emphasizes <em id="S3.SS2.p1.2.2" class="ltx_emph ltx_font_italic">personalized knowledge</em> tailored to the client’s task and distribution.
By merging them, <span id="S3.SS2.p1.2.3" class="ltx_text ltx_font_smallcaps">Potara</span> yields a client-specific model that simultaneously leverages federation and personalization, offering an effective trade-off between these two objectives.</p>
</div>
<div id="S3.SS2.p2" class="ltx_para">
<p id="S3.SS2.p2.1" class="ltx_p">Specifically, we denote the task vector <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_citep">(<a href="#bib.bib47" title="" class="ltx_ref">Ilharco et al., 2023</a>)</cite> of client <math id="S3.SS2.p2.m1" class="ltx_Math" alttext="i" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mi>i</mi><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">i</annotation></semantics></math>’s locally fine-tuned model as
<math id="S3.SS2.p2.m2" class="ltx_Math" alttext="\bm{\theta}^{(i)}_{\mathrm{Local}}=\mathbf{B}^{(i)}_{\mathrm{Local}}\mathbf{A}^{(i)}_{\mathrm{Local}}" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><msubsup><mi>𝜽</mi><mi>Local</mi><mrow><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mi>i</mi><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></mrow></msubsup><mo>=</mo><mrow><msubsup><mi>𝐁</mi><mi>Local</mi><mrow><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mi>i</mi><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></mrow></msubsup><mo lspace="0em" rspace="0em">​</mo><msubsup><mi>𝐀</mi><mi>Local</mi><mrow><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mi>i</mi><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></mrow></msubsup></mrow></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\bm{\theta}^{(i)}_{\mathrm{Local}}=\mathbf{B}^{(i)}_{\mathrm{Local}}\mathbf{A}^{(i)}_{\mathrm{Local}}</annotation></semantics></math>,
and the task vector of the FedIT model as
<math id="S3.SS2.p2.m3" class="ltx_Math" alttext="\bm{\theta}_{\mathrm{FedIT}}=\mathbf{B}_{\mathrm{FedIT}}\mathbf{A}_{\mathrm{FedIT}}" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><msub><mi>𝜽</mi><mi>FedIT</mi></msub><mo>=</mo><mrow><msub><mi>𝐁</mi><mi>FedIT</mi></msub><mo lspace="0em" rspace="0em">​</mo><msub><mi>𝐀</mi><mi>FedIT</mi></msub></mrow></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\bm{\theta}_{\mathrm{FedIT}}=\mathbf{B}_{\mathrm{FedIT}}\mathbf{A}_{\mathrm{FedIT}}</annotation></semantics></math>.
For each client <math id="S3.SS2.p2.m4" class="ltx_Math" alttext="i" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mi>i</mi><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">i</annotation></semantics></math>, we form the merged task vector by a convex combination:</p>
<table id="S3.EGx3" class="ltx_equationgroup ltx_eqn_align ltx_eqn_table">

<tbody id="S3.E3"><tr class="ltx_equation ltx_eqn_row ltx_align_baseline">
<td class="ltx_eqn_cell ltx_eqn_center_padleft"></td>
<td class="ltx_td ltx_align_right ltx_eqn_cell"><math id="S3.E3.m1" class="ltx_Math" alttext="\displaystyle\bm{\theta}^{(i)}_{\mathrm{Merge}}" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><msubsup><mi>𝜽</mi><mi>Merge</mi><mrow><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mi>i</mi><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></mrow></msubsup><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\displaystyle\bm{\theta}^{(i)}_{\mathrm{Merge}}</annotation></semantics></math></td>
<td class="ltx_td ltx_align_left ltx_eqn_cell"><math id="S3.E3.m2" class="ltx_Math" alttext="\displaystyle=\lambda^{(i)}_{\mathrm{FedIT}}\,\bm{\theta}_{\mathrm{FedIT}}+\lambda^{(i)}_{\mathrm{Local}}\,\bm{\theta}^{(i)}_{\mathrm{Local}}," display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><mrow><mphantom></mphantom><mo>=</mo><mrow><mrow><msubsup><mi>λ</mi><mi>FedIT</mi><mrow><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mi>i</mi><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></mrow></msubsup><mo lspace="0em" rspace="0em">​</mo><msub><mi>𝜽</mi><mi>FedIT</mi></msub></mrow><mo>+</mo><mrow><msubsup><mi>λ</mi><mi>Local</mi><mrow><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mi>i</mi><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></mrow></msubsup><mo lspace="0em" rspace="0em">​</mo><msubsup><mi>𝜽</mi><mi>Local</mi><mrow><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mi>i</mi><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></mrow></msubsup></mrow></mrow></mrow><mo>,</mo></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\displaystyle=\lambda^{(i)}_{\mathrm{FedIT}}\,\bm{\theta}_{\mathrm{FedIT}}+\lambda^{(i)}_{\mathrm{Local}}\,\bm{\theta}^{(i)}_{\mathrm{Local}},</annotation></semantics></math></td>
<td class="ltx_eqn_cell ltx_eqn_center_padright"></td>
<td rowspan="1" class="ltx_eqn_cell ltx_eqn_eqno ltx_align_middle ltx_align_right"><span class="ltx_tag ltx_tag_equation ltx_align_right">(3)</span></td></tr></tbody>
</table>
<p id="S3.SS2.p2.2" class="ltx_p">where <math id="S3.SS2.p2.m5" class="ltx_Math" alttext="\lambda^{(i)}_{\mathrm{FedIT}},\lambda^{(i)}_{\mathrm{Local}}\geq 0" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><msubsup><mi>λ</mi><mi>FedIT</mi><mrow><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mi>i</mi><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></mrow></msubsup><mo>,</mo><mrow><msubsup><mi>λ</mi><mi>Local</mi><mrow><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mi>i</mi><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></mrow></msubsup><mo>≥</mo><mn>0</mn></mrow></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\lambda^{(i)}_{\mathrm{FedIT}},\lambda^{(i)}_{\mathrm{Local}}\geq 0</annotation></semantics></math> denote the mixing weights for client <math id="S3.SS2.p2.m6" class="ltx_Math" alttext="i" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mi>i</mi><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">i</annotation></semantics></math> and <math id="S3.SS2.p2.m7" class="ltx_Math" alttext="\lambda^{(i)}_{\mathrm{FedIT}}+\lambda^{(i)}_{\mathrm{Local}}=1" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><mrow><msubsup><mi>λ</mi><mi>FedIT</mi><mrow><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mi>i</mi><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></mrow></msubsup><mo>+</mo><msubsup><mi>λ</mi><mi>Local</mi><mrow><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mi>i</mi><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></mrow></msubsup></mrow><mo>=</mo><mn>1</mn></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\lambda^{(i)}_{\mathrm{FedIT}}+\lambda^{(i)}_{\mathrm{Local}}=1</annotation></semantics></math>.
Then, the final model for each client is given by</p>
<table id="S3.EGx4" class="ltx_equationgroup ltx_eqn_align ltx_eqn_table">

<tbody id="S3.E4"><tr class="ltx_equation ltx_eqn_row ltx_align_baseline">
<td class="ltx_eqn_cell ltx_eqn_center_padleft"></td>
<td class="ltx_td ltx_align_right ltx_eqn_cell"><math id="S3.E4.m1" class="ltx_Math" alttext="\displaystyle\mathbf{W}_{\mathrm{Final}}^{(i)}=\mathbf{W}_{\mathrm{Pre}}+\bm{\theta}^{(i)}_{\mathrm{Merge}}." display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><mrow><msubsup><mi>𝐖</mi><mi>Final</mi><mrow><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mi>i</mi><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></mrow></msubsup><mo>=</mo><mrow><msub><mi>𝐖</mi><mi>Pre</mi></msub><mo>+</mo><msubsup><mi>𝜽</mi><mi>Merge</mi><mrow><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mi>i</mi><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></mrow></msubsup></mrow></mrow><mo lspace="0em">.</mo></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\displaystyle\mathbf{W}_{\mathrm{Final}}^{(i)}=\mathbf{W}_{\mathrm{Pre}}+\bm{\theta}^{(i)}_{\mathrm{Merge}}.</annotation></semantics></math></td>
<td class="ltx_eqn_cell ltx_eqn_center_padright"></td>
<td rowspan="1" class="ltx_eqn_cell ltx_eqn_eqno ltx_align_middle ltx_align_right"><span class="ltx_tag ltx_tag_equation ltx_align_right">(4)</span></td></tr></tbody>
</table>
</div>
<div id="S3.SS2.p3" class="ltx_para">
<p id="S3.SS2.p3.1" class="ltx_p">A natural question then arises: how to choose the mixing weights
<math id="S3.SS2.p3.m1" class="ltx_Math" alttext="\lambda^{(i)}_{\mathrm{FedIT}}" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><msubsup><mi>λ</mi><mi>FedIT</mi><mrow><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mi>i</mi><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></mrow></msubsup><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\lambda^{(i)}_{\mathrm{FedIT}}</annotation></semantics></math> and <math id="S3.SS2.p3.m2" class="ltx_Math" alttext="\lambda^{(i)}_{\mathrm{Local}}" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><msubsup><mi>λ</mi><mi>Local</mi><mrow><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mi>i</mi><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></mrow></msubsup><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\lambda^{(i)}_{\mathrm{Local}}</annotation></semantics></math>?
This choice is critical, as it governs the trade-off between leveraging <em id="S3.SS2.p3.1.1" class="ltx_emph ltx_font_italic">general knowledge</em> from FedIT and preserving <em id="S3.SS2.p3.1.2" class="ltx_emph ltx_font_italic">personalized knowledge</em> from local fine-tuning.
Next, we present our weighting strategy for determining <math id="S3.SS2.p3.m3" class="ltx_Math" alttext="\lambda^{(i)}_{\mathrm{FedIT}}" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><msubsup><mi>λ</mi><mi>FedIT</mi><mrow><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mi>i</mi><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></mrow></msubsup><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\lambda^{(i)}_{\mathrm{FedIT}}</annotation></semantics></math> and <math id="S3.SS2.p3.m4" class="ltx_Math" alttext="\lambda^{(i)}_{\mathrm{Local}}" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><msubsup><mi>λ</mi><mi>Local</mi><mrow><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mi>i</mi><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></mrow></msubsup><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\lambda^{(i)}_{\mathrm{Local}}</annotation></semantics></math> in a principled manner.</p>
</div>
</section>
<section id="S3.SS3" class="ltx_subsection">
<h3 class="ltx_title ltx_title_subsection"><span class="ltx_tag ltx_tag_subsection">3.3 </span>Determination of Mixing Weights</h3>

<div id="S3.SS3.p1" class="ltx_para">
<p id="S3.SS3.p1.1" class="ltx_p">In the preliminaries, we recalled the standard definition of LMC, which characterizes the phenomenon in terms of the loss remaining nearly constant along the linear interpolation path.
To obtain a local geometric characterization of LMC, we introduce the notion of LMC basin below.</p>
</div>
<div id="S3.Thmtheorem1" class="ltx_theorem ltx_theorem_definition">
<h6 class="ltx_title ltx_runin ltx_title_theorem"><span class="ltx_tag ltx_tag_theorem"><span id="S3.Thmtheorem1.2" class="ltx_text ltx_font_bold">Definition 3.1</span></span><span id="S3.Thmtheorem1.3" class="ltx_text ltx_font_bold">.</span></h6>
<div id="S3.Thmtheorem1.p1" class="ltx_para">
<p id="S3.Thmtheorem1.p1.1" class="ltx_p">For a given radius <math id="S3.Thmtheorem1.p1.m1" class="ltx_Math" alttext="\delta&gt;0" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><mi>δ</mi><mo>&gt;</mo><mn>0</mn></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\delta&gt;0</annotation></semantics></math>, define the LMC basin around the optimum <math id="S3.Thmtheorem1.p1.m2" class="ltx_Math" alttext="\mathbf{W}^{*}" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><msup><mi>𝐖</mi><mo>∗</mo></msup><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\mathbf{W}^{*}</annotation></semantics></math> as</p>
<table id="S3.EGx5" class="ltx_equationgroup ltx_eqn_align ltx_eqn_table">

<tbody id="S3.E5"><tr class="ltx_equation ltx_eqn_row ltx_align_baseline">
<td class="ltx_eqn_cell ltx_eqn_center_padleft"></td>
<td class="ltx_td ltx_align_right ltx_eqn_cell"><math id="S3.E5.m1" class="ltx_Math" alttext="\displaystyle\mathcal{U}_{\delta}=\big\{\mathbf{W}:\ \|\mathbf{W}-\mathbf{W}^{*}\|\leq\delta\big\}." display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><mrow><msub><mi class="ltx_font_mathcaligraphic">𝒰</mi><mi>δ</mi></msub><mo>=</mo><mrow><mo stretchy="false">{</mo><mi>𝐖</mi><mo lspace="0.278em" rspace="0.778em">:</mo><mrow><mrow><mo stretchy="false">‖</mo><mrow><mi>𝐖</mi><mo>−</mo><msup><mi>𝐖</mi><mo>∗</mo></msup></mrow><mo stretchy="false">‖</mo></mrow><mo>≤</mo><mi>δ</mi></mrow><mo stretchy="false">}</mo></mrow></mrow><mo lspace="0em">.</mo></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\displaystyle\mathcal{U}_{\delta}=\big\{\mathbf{W}:\ \|\mathbf{W}-\mathbf{W}^{*}\|\leq\delta\big\}.</annotation></semantics></math></td>
<td class="ltx_eqn_cell ltx_eqn_center_padright"></td>
<td rowspan="1" class="ltx_eqn_cell ltx_eqn_eqno ltx_align_middle ltx_align_right"><span class="ltx_tag ltx_tag_equation ltx_align_right">(5)</span></td></tr></tbody>
</table>
<p id="S3.Thmtheorem1.p1.2" class="ltx_p">Two models <math id="S3.Thmtheorem1.p1.m3" class="ltx_Math" alttext="\mathbf{W}_{1}" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><msub><mi>𝐖</mi><mn>1</mn></msub><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\mathbf{W}_{1}</annotation></semantics></math> and <math id="S3.Thmtheorem1.p1.m4" class="ltx_Math" alttext="\mathbf{W}_{2}" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><msub><mi>𝐖</mi><mn>2</mn></msub><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\mathbf{W}_{2}</annotation></semantics></math> exhibit linear mode connectivity in <math id="S3.Thmtheorem1.p1.m5" class="ltx_Math" alttext="\mathcal{U}_{\delta}" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><msub><mi class="ltx_font_mathcaligraphic">𝒰</mi><mi>δ</mi></msub><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\mathcal{U}_{\delta}</annotation></semantics></math>
if all their convex combination lies entirely in <math id="S3.Thmtheorem1.p1.m6" class="ltx_Math" alttext="\mathcal{U}_{\delta}" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><msub><mi class="ltx_font_mathcaligraphic">𝒰</mi><mi>δ</mi></msub><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\mathcal{U}_{\delta}</annotation></semantics></math>, i.e.,</p>
<table id="S3.EGx6" class="ltx_equationgroup ltx_eqn_align ltx_eqn_table">

<tbody id="S3.E6"><tr class="ltx_equation ltx_eqn_row ltx_align_baseline">
