</div>
<div id="A1.Thmtheorem2" class="ltx_theorem ltx_theorem_lemma">
<h6 class="ltx_title ltx_runin ltx_title_theorem"><span class="ltx_tag ltx_tag_theorem"><span id="A1.Thmtheorem2.2" class="ltx_text ltx_font_bold">Lemma A.2</span></span><span id="A1.Thmtheorem2.3" class="ltx_text ltx_font_bold">.</span></h6>
<div id="A1.Thmtheorem2.p1" class="ltx_para">
<p id="A1.Thmtheorem2.p1.1" class="ltx_p"><span id="A1.Thmtheorem2.p1.1.1" class="ltx_text ltx_font_italic">Assume <math id="A1.Thmtheorem2.p1.m1" class="ltx_Math" alttext="\begin{bmatrix}\bm{\Sigma}_{1}&amp;\bm{\Sigma}_{12}\\
\bm{\Sigma}_{12}^{\top}&amp;\bm{\Sigma}_{2}\end{bmatrix}\succeq 0." display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><mrow><mrow><mo>[</mo><mtable columnspacing="5pt" rowspacing="0pt"><mtr><mtd><msub><mi>𝚺</mi><mn>1</mn></msub></mtd><mtd><msub><mi>𝚺</mi><mn>12</mn></msub></mtd></mtr><mtr><mtd><msubsup><mi>𝚺</mi><mn>12</mn><mo>⊤</mo></msubsup></mtd><mtd><msub><mi>𝚺</mi><mn>2</mn></msub></mtd></mtr></mtable><mo>]</mo></mrow><mo>⪰</mo><mn>0</mn></mrow><mo lspace="0em">.</mo></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\begin{bmatrix}\bm{\Sigma}_{1}&amp;\bm{\Sigma}_{12}\\
\bm{\Sigma}_{12}^{\top}&amp;\bm{\Sigma}_{2}\end{bmatrix}\succeq 0.</annotation></semantics></math> Then</span></p>
<table id="A1.EGx43" class="ltx_equationgroup ltx_eqn_align ltx_eqn_table">

<tbody id="A1.E49"><tr class="ltx_equation ltx_eqn_row ltx_align_baseline">

<td class="ltx_eqn_cell ltx_eqn_center_padright"></td>

</div>

<div id="A1.SS4.3" class="ltx_proof">
<h6 class="ltx_title ltx_runin ltx_font_italic ltx_title_proof">Proof.</h6>
<div id="A1.SS4.p2" class="ltx_para">
<p id="A1.SS4.p2.1" class="ltx_p"><span id="A1.SS4.p2.1.1" class="ltx_text">Since
<math id="A1.SS4.p2.m1" class="ltx_Math" alttext="\begin{bmatrix}\bm{\Sigma}_{1}&amp;\bm{\Sigma}_{12}\\
\bm{\Sigma}_{12}^{\top}&amp;\bm{\Sigma}_{2}\end{bmatrix}\succeq 0," display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><mrow><mrow><mo>[</mo><mtable columnspacing="5pt" rowspacing="0pt"><mtr><mtd><msub><mi>𝚺</mi><mn>1</mn></msub></mtd><mtd><msub><mi>𝚺</mi><mn>12</mn></msub></mtd></mtr><mtr><mtd><msubsup><mi>𝚺</mi><mn>12</mn><mo>⊤</mo></msubsup></mtd><mtd><msub><mi>𝚺</mi><mn>2</mn></msub></mtd></mtr></mtable><mo>]</mo></mrow><mo>⪰</mo><mn>0</mn></mrow><mo>,</mo></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\begin{bmatrix}\bm{\Sigma}_{1}&amp;\bm{\Sigma}_{12}\\
\bm{\Sigma}_{12}^{\top}&amp;\bm{\Sigma}_{2}\end{bmatrix}\succeq 0,</annotation></semantics></math>
there exists a matrix <math id="A1.SS4.p2.m2" class="ltx_Math" alttext="\mathbf{R}" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mi>𝐑</mi><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\mathbf{R}</annotation></semantics></math> with <math id="A1.SS4.p2.m3" class="ltx_Math" alttext="\|\mathbf{R}\|_{2}\leq 1" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><msub><mrow><mo stretchy="false">‖</mo><mi>𝐑</mi><mo stretchy="false">‖</mo></mrow><mn>2</mn></msub><mo>≤</mo><mn>1</mn></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\|\mathbf{R}\|_{2}\leq 1</annotation></semantics></math> such that</span></p>
<table id="A1.EGx44" class="ltx_equationgroup ltx_eqn_align ltx_eqn_table">

<tbody id="A1.E50"><tr class="ltx_equation ltx_eqn_row ltx_align_baseline">
<td class="ltx_eqn_cell ltx_eqn_center_padleft"></td>

<td class="ltx_eqn_cell ltx_eqn_center_padright"></td>

</table>
<p id="A1.SS4.p2.2" class="ltx_p"><span id="A1.SS4.p2.2.1" class="ltx_text">By applying trace,</span></p>

<td rowspan="1" class="ltx_eqn_cell ltx_eqn_eqno ltx_align_middle ltx_align_right"><span class="ltx_tag ltx_tag_equation ltx_align_right">(51)</span></td></tr></tbody>
</table>
<p id="A1.SS4.p2.3" class="ltx_p"><span id="A1.SS4.p2.3.1" class="ltx_text">Using the trace inequality <math id="A1.SS4.p2.m4" class="ltx_Math" alttext="|\mathrm{tr}(\mathbf{A}^{\top}\mathbf{B})|\leq\|\mathbf{A}\|_{F}\|\mathbf{B}\|_{F}" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><mrow><mo stretchy="false">|</mo><mrow><mi>tr</mi><mo>⁡</mo><mrow><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mrow><msup><mi>𝐀</mi><mo>⊤</mo></msup><mo lspace="0em" rspace="0em">​</mo><mi>𝐁</mi></mrow><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></mrow></mrow><mo stretchy="false">|</mo></mrow><mo>≤</mo><mrow><msub><mrow><mo stretchy="false">‖</mo><mi>𝐀</mi><mo stretchy="false">‖</mo></mrow><mi>F</mi></msub><mo lspace="0em" rspace="0em">​</mo><msub><mrow><mo stretchy="false">‖</mo><mi>𝐁</mi><mo stretchy="false">‖</mo></mrow><mi>F</mi></msub></mrow></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">|\mathrm{tr}(\mathbf{A}^{\top}\mathbf{B})|\leq\|\mathbf{A}\|_{F}\|\mathbf{B}\|_{F}</annotation></semantics></math> and
<math id="A1.SS4.p2.m5" class="ltx_Math" alttext="\|\mathbf{R}X\|_{F}\leq\|\mathbf{R}\|_{2}\|X\|_{F}" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><msub><mrow><mo stretchy="false">‖</mo><mrow><mi>𝐑</mi><mo lspace="0em" rspace="0em">​</mo><mi>X</mi></mrow><mo stretchy="false">‖</mo></mrow><mi>F</mi></msub><mo>≤</mo><mrow><msub><mrow><mo stretchy="false">‖</mo><mi>𝐑</mi><mo stretchy="false">‖</mo></mrow><mn>2</mn></msub><mo lspace="0em" rspace="0em">​</mo><msub><mrow><mo stretchy="false">‖</mo><mi>X</mi><mo stretchy="false">‖</mo></mrow><mi>F</mi></msub></mrow></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\|\mathbf{R}X\|_{F}\leq\|\mathbf{R}\|_{2}\|X\|_{F}</annotation></semantics></math>, we have</span></p>

<p id="A1.SS4.p2.4" class="ltx_p"><span id="A1.SS4.p2.4.1" class="ltx_text">Note that <math id="A1.SS4.p2.m6" class="ltx_Math" alttext="\|\bm{\Sigma}_{1}^{1/2}\|_{F}^{2}=\mathrm{tr}((\bm{\Sigma}_{1}^{1/2})^{\top}\bm{\Sigma}_{1}^{1/2})=\mathrm{tr}(\bm{\Sigma}_{1}^{1/2}\bm{\Sigma}_{1}^{1/2})=\mathrm{tr}(\bm{\Sigma}_{1})." display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><mrow><msubsup><mrow><mo stretchy="false">‖</mo><msubsup><mi>𝚺</mi><mn>1</mn><mrow><mn>1</mn><mo>/</mo><mn>2</mn></mrow></msubsup><mo stretchy="false">‖</mo></mrow><mi>F</mi><mn>2</mn></msubsup><mo>=</mo><mrow><mi>tr</mi><mo>⁡</mo><mrow><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mrow><msup><mrow><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><msubsup><mi>𝚺</mi><mn>1</mn><mrow><mn>1</mn><mo>/</mo><mn>2</mn></mrow></msubsup><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></mrow><mo>⊤</mo></msup><mo lspace="0em" rspace="0em">​</mo><msubsup><mi>𝚺</mi><mn>1</mn><mrow><mn>1</mn><mo>/</mo><mn>2</mn></mrow></msubsup></mrow><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></mrow></mrow><mo>=</mo><mrow><mi>tr</mi><mo>⁡</mo><mrow><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mrow><msubsup><mi>𝚺</mi><mn>1</mn><mrow><mn>1</mn><mo>/</mo><mn>2</mn></mrow></msubsup><mo lspace="0em" rspace="0em">​</mo><msubsup><mi>𝚺</mi><mn>1</mn><mrow><mn>1</mn><mo>/</mo><mn>2</mn></mrow></msubsup></mrow><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></mrow></mrow><mo>=</mo><mrow><mi>tr</mi><mo>⁡</mo><mrow><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><msub><mi>𝚺</mi><mn>1</mn></msub><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></mrow></mrow></mrow><mo lspace="0em">.</mo></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\|\bm{\Sigma}_{1}^{1/2}\|_{F}^{2}=\mathrm{tr}((\bm{\Sigma}_{1}^{1/2})^{\top}\bm{\Sigma}_{1}^{1/2})=\mathrm{tr}(\bm{\Sigma}_{1}^{1/2}\bm{\Sigma}_{1}^{1/2})=\mathrm{tr}(\bm{\Sigma}_{1}).</annotation></semantics></math>
Similarly,
<math id="A1.SS4.p2.m7" class="ltx_Math" alttext="\|\bm{\Sigma}_{2}^{1/2}\|_{F}^{2}=\mathrm{tr}(\bm{\Sigma}_{2})" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><msubsup><mrow><mo stretchy="false">‖</mo><msubsup><mi>𝚺</mi><mn>2</mn><mrow><mn>1</mn><mo>/</mo><mn>2</mn></mrow></msubsup><mo stretchy="false">‖</mo></mrow><mi>F</mi><mn>2</mn></msubsup><mo>=</mo><mrow><mi>tr</mi><mo>⁡</mo><mrow><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><msub><mi>𝚺</mi><mn>2</mn></msub><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></mrow></mrow></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\|\bm{\Sigma}_{2}^{1/2}\|_{F}^{2}=\mathrm{tr}(\bm{\Sigma}_{2})</annotation></semantics></math>.
Therefore,</span></p>

<tbody><tr class="ltx_equation ltx_eqn_row ltx_align_baseline">
<td class="ltx_eqn_cell ltx_eqn_center_padleft"></td>
<td class="ltx_eqn_cell ltx_align_center"><math id="A1.Ex20.m1" class="ltx_Math" alttext="\big|\mathrm{tr}(\bm{\Sigma}_{12})\big|\leq\sqrt{\mathrm{tr}(\bm{\Sigma}_{1})\,\mathrm{tr}(\bm{\Sigma}_{2})}." display="block" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><mrow><mrow><mo maxsize="1.200em" minsize="1.200em" stretchy="true">|</mo><mrow><mi>tr</mi><mo>⁡</mo><mrow><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><msub><mi>𝚺</mi><mn>12</mn></msub><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></mrow></mrow><mo maxsize="1.200em" minsize="1.200em" stretchy="true">|</mo></mrow><mo>≤</mo><msqrt><mrow><mrow><mi>tr</mi><mo>⁡</mo><mrow><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><msub><mi>𝚺</mi><mn>1</mn></msub><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></mrow></mrow><mo lspace="0.170em" rspace="0em">​</mo><mi>tr</mi><mo lspace="0em" rspace="0em">​</mo><mrow><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><msub><mi>𝚺</mi><mn>2</mn></msub><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></mrow></mrow></msqrt></mrow><mo lspace="0em">.</mo></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\big|\mathrm{tr}(\bm{\Sigma}_{12})\big|\leq\sqrt{\mathrm{tr}(\bm{\Sigma}_{1})\,\mathrm{tr}(\bm{\Sigma}_{2})}.</annotation></semantics></math></td>

<section id="A2" class="ltx_appendix">
<h2 class="ltx_title ltx_title_appendix"><span class="ltx_tag ltx_tag_appendix">Appendix B </span>Implementation</h2>

<div id="A2.p1" class="ltx_para">
<p id="A2.p1.1" class="ltx_p">Let <math id="A2.p1.m1" class="ltx_Math" alttext="\{(\mathbf{x}_{n},\mathbf{y}_{n})\}_{n=1}^{N}" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><msubsup><mrow><mo stretchy="false">{</mo><mrow><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><msub><mi>𝐱</mi><mi>n</mi></msub><mo>,</mo><msub><mi>𝐲</mi><mi>n</mi></msub><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></mrow><mo stretchy="false">}</mo></mrow><mrow><mi>n</mi><mo>=</mo><mn>1</mn></mrow><mi>N</mi></msubsup><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\{(\mathbf{x}_{n},\mathbf{y}_{n})\}_{n=1}^{N}</annotation></semantics></math> be a random data batch from training set of client <math id="A2.p1.m2" class="ltx_Math" alttext="i" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mi>i</mi><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">i</annotation></semantics></math>.
For two well-trained models with parameters <math id="A2.p1.m3" class="ltx_Math" alttext="\bm{\mu}_{\mathrm{FedIT}}" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><msub><mi>𝝁</mi><mi>FedIT</mi></msub><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\bm{\mu}_{\mathrm{FedIT}}</annotation></semantics></math> and <math id="A2.p1.m4" class="ltx_Math" alttext="\bm{\mu}_{\mathrm{Local}}" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><msub><mi>𝝁</mi><mi>Local</mi></msub><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\bm{\mu}_{\mathrm{Local}}</annotation></semantics></math>, the per-sample gradients are given by</p>
<table id="A2.EGx47" class="ltx_equationgroup ltx_eqn_align ltx_eqn_table">

<tbody id="A2.E53"><tr class="ltx_equation ltx_eqn_row ltx_align_baseline">
<td class="ltx_eqn_cell ltx_eqn_center_padleft"></td>

<p id="A2.p1.2" class="ltx_p">where <math id="A2.p1.m5" class="ltx_Math" alttext="\ell" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mi mathvariant="normal">ℓ</mi><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\ell</annotation></semantics></math> is the per-sample task loss. For each parameter coordinate <math id="A2.p1.m6" class="ltx_Math" alttext="k\in\{1,\dots,d\}" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><mi>k</mi><mo>∈</mo><mrow><mo stretchy="false">{</mo><mrow><mn>1</mn><mo>,</mo><mi mathvariant="normal">…</mi><mo>,</mo><mi>d</mi></mrow><mo stretchy="false">}</mo></mrow></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">k\in\{1,\dots,d\}</annotation></semantics></math>, compute the mean and variance of per-sample gradient, and covariance as</p>

<p id="A2.p1.3" class="ltx_p">The gradient correlation coefficient for coordinate <math id="A2.p1.m7" class="ltx_Math" alttext="k" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mi>k</mi><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">k</annotation></semantics></math> is defined as</p>

<p id="A2.p1.5" class="ltx_p">and clip <math id="A2.p1.m8" class="ltx_Math" alttext="\rho_{k}" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><msub><mi>ρ</mi><mi>k</mi></msub><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\rho_{k}</annotation></semantics></math> to ensure <math id="A2.p1.m9" class="ltx_Math" alttext="\bm{\Sigma}_{\mathrm{Cross}}\succeq 0" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><msub><mi>𝚺</mi><mi>Cross</mi></msub><mo>⪰</mo><mn>0</mn></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\bm{\Sigma}_{\mathrm{Cross}}\succeq 0</annotation></semantics></math> and <math id="A2.p1.m10" class="ltx_Math" alttext="\bm{\Sigma}_{\mathrm{Cross}}\preceq\bm{\Sigma}_{\mathrm{FedIT}},\bm{\Sigma}_{\mathrm{Local}}" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><mrow><msub><mi>𝚺</mi><mi>Cross</mi></msub><mo>⪯</mo><msub><mi>𝚺</mi><mi>FedIT</mi></msub></mrow><mo>,</mo><msub><mi>𝚺</mi><mi>Local</mi></msub></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\bm{\Sigma}_{\mathrm{Cross}}\preceq\bm{\Sigma}_{\mathrm{FedIT}},\bm{\Sigma}_{\mathrm{Local}}</annotation></semantics></math>:</p>

<td rowspan="1" class="ltx_eqn_cell ltx_eqn_eqno ltx_align_middle ltx_align_right"><span class="ltx_tag ltx_tag_equation ltx_align_right">(58)</span></td></tr></tbody>
</table>
<p id="A2.p1.6" class="ltx_p">This yields a PSD diagonal <math id="A2.p1.m11" class="ltx_Math" alttext="\bm{\Sigma}_{\mathrm{Cross}}" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><msub><mi>𝚺</mi><mi>Cross</mi></msub><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\bm{\Sigma}_{\mathrm{Cross}}</annotation></semantics></math> with each element bounded by the corresponding entries of <math id="A2.p1.m12" class="ltx_Math" alttext="\bm{\Sigma}_{\mathrm{FedIT}}" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><msub><mi>𝚺</mi><mi>FedIT</mi></msub><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\bm{\Sigma}_{\mathrm{FedIT}}</annotation></semantics></math> and <math id="A2.p1.m13" class="ltx_Math" alttext="\bm{\Sigma}_{\mathrm{Local}}" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><msub><mi>𝚺</mi><mi>Local</mi></msub><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\bm{\Sigma}_{\mathrm{Local}}</annotation></semantics></math>.</p>
</div>
<div id="A2.p2" class="ltx_para">
<p id="A2.p2.1" class="ltx_p">Then, we calculate the scalar <math id="A2.p2.m1" class="ltx_Math" alttext="c" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mi>c</mi><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">c</annotation></semantics></math> as</p>
<table id="A2.EGx53" class="ltx_equationgroup ltx_eqn_align ltx_eqn_table">

<tbody id="A2.E59"><tr class="ltx_equation ltx_eqn_row ltx_align_baseline">
<td class="ltx_eqn_cell ltx_eqn_center_padleft"></td>
<td class="ltx_td ltx_align_right ltx_eqn_cell"><math id="A2.E59.m1" class="ltx_Math" alttext="\displaystyle c\;\triangleq\;\mathrm{tr}(\bm{\Sigma}_{\mathrm{Cross}})\,=\,\sum_{k=1}^{d}\,(\bm{\Sigma}_{\mathrm{Cross}})_{kk}\,=\,\sum_{k=1}^{d}\,\rho_{k}\,\sqrt{(\bm{\Sigma}_{\mathrm{FedIT}})_{kk}\,(\bm{\Sigma}_{\mathrm{Local}})_{kk}}" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><mi>c</mi><mo lspace="0.558em" rspace="0.558em">≜</mo><mrow><mi>tr</mi><mo>⁡</mo><mrow><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><msub><mi>𝚺</mi><mi>Cross</mi></msub><mo rspace="0.170em" stretchy="false">)</mo></mrow></mrow><mo rspace="0.448em">=</mo><mrow><mstyle displaystyle="true"><munderover><mo movablelimits="false">∑</mo><mrow><mi>k</mi><mo>=</mo><mn>1</mn></mrow><mi>d</mi></munderover></mstyle><msub><mrow><mo lspace="0.170em" stretchy="false">(</mo><msub><mi>𝚺</mi><mi>Cross</mi></msub><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></mrow><mrow><mi>k</mi><mo lspace="0em" rspace="0em">​</mo><mi>k</mi></mrow></msub></mrow><mo rspace="0.448em">=</mo><mrow><mstyle displaystyle="true"><munderover><mo movablelimits="false">∑</mo><mrow><mi>k</mi><mo>=</mo><mn>1</mn></mrow><mi>d</mi></munderover></mstyle><mrow><msub><mi>ρ</mi><mi>k</mi></msub><mo lspace="0em" rspace="0em">​</mo><msqrt><mrow><msub><mrow><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><msub><mi>𝚺</mi><mi>FedIT</mi></msub><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></mrow><mrow><mi>k</mi><mo lspace="0em" rspace="0em">​</mo><mi>k</mi></mrow></msub><mo lspace="0.170em" rspace="0em">​</mo><msub><mrow><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><msub><mi>𝚺</mi><mi>Local</mi></msub><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></mrow><mrow><mi>k</mi><mo lspace="0em" rspace="0em">​</mo><mi>k</mi></mrow></msub></mrow></msqrt></mrow></mrow></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\displaystyle c\;\triangleq\;\mathrm{tr}(\bm{\Sigma}_{\mathrm{Cross}})\,=\,\sum_{k=1}^{d}\,(\bm{\Sigma}_{\mathrm{Cross}})_{kk}\,=\,\sum_{k=1}^{d}\,\rho_{k}\,\sqrt{(\bm{\Sigma}_{\mathrm{FedIT}})_{kk}\,(\bm{\Sigma}_{\mathrm{Local}})_{kk}}</annotation></semantics></math></td>
<td class="ltx_eqn_cell ltx_eqn_center_padright"></td>
<td rowspan="1" class="ltx_eqn_cell ltx_eqn_eqno ltx_align_middle ltx_align_right"><span class="ltx_tag ltx_tag_equation ltx_align_right">(59)</span></td></tr></tbody>
</table>
</div>
<div id="A2.p3" class="ltx_para">
<p id="A2.p3.1" class="ltx_p">Note that in practice <math id="A2.p3.m1" class="ltx_Math" alttext="\bm{\theta}" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mi>𝜽</mi><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\bm{\theta}</annotation></semantics></math> is parameterized by
LoRA modules <math id="A2.p3.m2" class="ltx_Math" alttext="\{\mathbf{B},\mathbf{A}\}" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><mo stretchy="false">{</mo><mi>𝐁</mi><mo>,</mo><mi>𝐀</mi><mo stretchy="false">}</mo></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\{\mathbf{B},\mathbf{A}\}</annotation></semantics></math> and the actual trainable parameters
are <math id="A2.p3.m3" class="ltx_Math" alttext="\mathbf{B}" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mi>𝐁</mi><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\mathbf{B}</annotation></semantics></math> and <math id="A2.p3.m4" class="ltx_Math" alttext="\mathbf{A}" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mi>𝐀</mi><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\mathbf{A}</annotation></semantics></math>.
Therefore, the Fisher information matrix in
Eq. (<a href="#S3.E19" title="Equation 19 ‣ 3.4 Estimation of Fisher Information Matrix ‣ 3 Our Method: Potara ‣ Communication-Efficient Personalized Adaptation via Federated-Local Model Merging" class="ltx_ref"><span class="ltx_text ltx_ref_tag">19</span></a>) is estimated with respect to the LoRA parameters
<math id="A2.p3.m5" class="ltx_Math" alttext="\{\mathbf{B},\mathbf{A}\}" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><mo stretchy="false">{</mo><mi>𝐁</mi><mo>,</mo><mi>𝐀</mi><mo stretchy="false">}</mo></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\{\mathbf{B},\mathbf{A}\}</annotation></semantics></math> rather than the composed matrix product <math id="A2.p3.m6" class="ltx_Math" alttext="\mathbf{B}\mathbf{A}" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mi>𝐁𝐀</mi><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\mathbf{B}\mathbf{A}</annotation></semantics></math>.
Accordingly, we estimate the diagonal Fisher information for
<math id="A2.p3.m7" class="ltx_Math" alttext="\mathbf{B}" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mi>𝐁</mi><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\mathbf{B}</annotation></semantics></math> and <math id="A2.p3.m8" class="ltx_Math" alttext="\mathbf{A}" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mi>𝐀</mi><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\mathbf{A}</annotation></semantics></math>, and perform merging separately for <math id="A2.p3.m9" class="ltx_Math" alttext="\mathbf{B}" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mi>𝐁</mi><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\mathbf{B}</annotation></semantics></math> and <math id="A2.p3.m10" class="ltx_Math" alttext="\mathbf{A}" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mi>𝐀</mi><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\mathbf{A}</annotation></semantics></math>, instead of first forming <math id="A2.p3.m11" class="ltx_Math" alttext="\bm{\theta}=\mathbf{B}\mathbf{A}" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><mi>𝜽</mi><mo>=</mo><mi>𝐁𝐀</mi></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\bm{\theta}=\mathbf{B}\mathbf{A}</annotation></semantics></math> and computing its Fisher information.</p>
</div>
<div class="ltx_pagination ltx_role_newpage"></div>
</section>
<section id="A3" class="ltx_appendix">
<h2 class="ltx_title ltx_title_appendix"><span class="ltx_tag ltx_tag_appendix">Appendix C </span>Experiments on FLAN benchmark</h2>

<section id="A3.SS1" class="ltx_subsection">
<h3 class="ltx_title ltx_title_subsection"><span class="ltx_tag ltx_tag_subsection">C.1 </span>Performance Comparison</h3>

<div id="A3.SS1.p1" class="ltx_para">
<p id="A3.SS1.p1.1" class="ltx_p">We evaluate <span id="A3.SS1.p1.1.1" class="ltx_text ltx_font_smallcaps">Potara</span> on the FLAN benchmark <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_citep">(<a href="#bib.bib26" title="" class="ltx_ref">Chung et al., 2024</a>)</cite>, which consists of over 60 datasets covering more than 12 NLP task categories.
To simulate an extreme heterogeneity scenario, we consider eight clients, each trained on a completely different dataset.
This setting is highly task-heterogeneous and is substantially more extreme than the CIFAR-100 and commonsense reasoning setups.
Dataset details, task descriptions, and client assignments are summarized in Appendix <a href="#A3.SS2" title="C.2 FLAN benchmark ‣ Appendix C Experiments on FLAN benchmark ‣ Communication-Efficient Personalized Adaptation via Federated-Local Model Merging" class="ltx_ref"><span class="ltx_text ltx_ref_tag">C.2</span></a>.
We adopt Qwen3-4B-Instruct-2507 <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_citep">(<a href="#bib.bib27" title="" class="ltx_ref">Yang et al., 2025</a>)</cite> as the pre-trained model and report ROUGE-1 for all tasks.
Baselines are trained for 600 rounds, except local fine-tuning which runs for 300 rounds to mitigate overfitting.
For <span id="A3.SS1.p1.1.2" class="ltx_text ltx_font_smallcaps">Potara</span>, we train FedIT for 300 rounds and local fine-tuning for 300 rounds, and merge the two resulting models to obtain the final model.
As shown in Table <a href="#A3.T6" title="Table 6 ‣ C.1 Performance Comparison ‣ Appendix C Experiments on FLAN benchmark ‣ Communication-Efficient Personalized Adaptation via Federated-Local Model Merging" class="ltx_ref"><span class="ltx_text ltx_ref_tag">6</span></a>, <span id="A3.SS1.p1.1.3" class="ltx_text ltx_font_smallcaps">Potara</span> achieves the best overall ROUGE-1 on the FLAN benchmark and consistently performing strongly across diverse task categories, indicating that merging global knowledge with personalized knowledge is especially effective under extreme task heterogeneity.
Meanwhile, <span id="A3.SS1.p1.1.4" class="ltx_text ltx_font_smallcaps">Potara</span> attains these improvements while reducing communication cost because it merges an intermediate FedIT model with local model.</p>
</div>

<section id="A3.SS2" class="ltx_subsection">
<h3 class="ltx_title ltx_title_subsection"><span class="ltx_tag ltx_tag_subsection">C.2 </span>FLAN benchmark</h3>

<div id="A3.SS2.p1" class="ltx_para">
<p id="A3.SS2.p1.1" class="ltx_p">We follow the experimental setup in <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_citep">(<a href="#bib.bib46" title="" class="ltx_ref">Bian et al., 2026</a>; <a href="#bib.bib48" title="" class="ltx_ref">Yang et al., 2024</a>)</cite> to simulate a client-level task heterogeneity setting using the FLAN datasets <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_citep">(<a href="#bib.bib26" title="" class="ltx_ref">Chung et al., 2024</a>)</cite>.
The FLAN collection comprises over 12 natural language processing tasks, each of which contains multiple datasets.
These tasks are generated from diverse contextual factors and inherently exhibit complex and heterogeneous data distribution shifts.
We consider an extreme client heterogeneity setting where 8 clients are assigned completely different NLP tasks.
To simulate a realistic environment where each client has limited access to large-scale datasets, we adopt a downsampling strategy that assigns 2000 training samples and 300 test samples to each client.
The specific task and dataset assignments are summarized in Table <a href="#A3.T7" title="Table 7 ‣ C.2 FLAN benchmark ‣ Appendix C Experiments on FLAN benchmark ‣ Communication-Efficient Personalized Adaptation via Federated-Local Model Merging" class="ltx_ref"><span class="ltx_text ltx_ref_tag">7</span></a>.</p>
</div>

<section id="A4" class="ltx_appendix">
<h2 class="ltx_title ltx_title_appendix"><span class="ltx_tag ltx_tag_appendix">Appendix D </span>Experiments with Increased Number of Clients</h2>

<div id="A4.p1" class="ltx_para">
<p id="A4.p1.1" class="ltx_p">In this section, we extend our experiments to settings with a larger number of clients.
For the personalized CIFAR-100 benchmark, we increase the number of clients to 20, with each client following a distinct label distribution.
For the commonsense reasoning benchmark, we increase the number of clients to 16, where every two clients share the same task but have different training samples.
Table <a href="#A4.T8" title="Table 8 ‣ Appendix D Experiments with Increased Number of Clients ‣ Communication-Efficient Personalized Adaptation via Federated-Local Model Merging" class="ltx_ref"><span class="ltx_text ltx_ref_tag">8</span></a> and <a href="#A4.T9" title="Table 9 ‣ Appendix D Experiments with Increased Number of Clients ‣ Communication-Efficient Personalized Adaptation via Federated-Local Model Merging" class="ltx_ref"><span class="ltx_text ltx_ref_tag">9</span></a> show that with increased number of clients, <span id="A4.p1.1.1" class="ltx_text ltx_font_smallcaps">Potara</span> consistently outperforms all baselines, demonstrating robust performance gains at larger scale.</p>
</div>

<section id="A5" class="ltx_appendix">
<h2 class="ltx_title ltx_title_appendix"><span class="ltx_tag ltx_tag_appendix">Appendix E </span>Client Performance with Various Mixing Weight</h2>

<div id="A5.p1" class="ltx_para">
<p id="A5.p1.1" class="ltx_p">In this section, we investigate the effect of the mixing weight <math id="A5.p1.m1" class="ltx_Math" alttext="\lambda" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mi>λ</mi><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\lambda</annotation></semantics></math> that balances the FedIT model and the local fine-tuning model in the proposed <span id="A5.p1.1.1" class="ltx_text ltx_font_smallcaps">Potara</span> framework.
Specifically, we vary <math id="A5.p1.m2" class="ltx_Math" alttext="\lambda\in\{0,0.1,\ldots,1\}" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><mi>λ</mi><mo>∈</mo><mrow><mo stretchy="false">{</mo><mrow><mn>0</mn><mo>,</mo><mn>0.1</mn><mo>,</mo><mi mathvariant="normal">…</mi><mo>,</mo><mn>1</mn></mrow><mo stretchy="false">}</mo></mrow></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\lambda\in\{0,0.1,\ldots,1\}</annotation></semantics></math> and evaluate client-wise performance under different mixing weights, where <math id="A5.p1.m3" class="ltx_Math" alttext="\lambda=1" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><mi>λ</mi><mo>=</mo><mn>1</mn></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\lambda=1</annotation></semantics></math> corresponds to using the FedIT model alone and <math id="A5.p1.m4" class="ltx_Math" alttext="\lambda=0" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><mi>λ</mi><mo>=</mo><mn>0</mn></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\lambda=0</annotation></semantics></math> corresponds to purely local fine-tuning.
We conduct this analysis on commonsense reasoning benchmark with LLaMA.
Figure <a href="#A5.F4" title="Figure 4 ‣ Appendix E Client Performance with Various Mixing Weight ‣ Communication-Efficient Personalized Adaptation via Federated-Local Model Merging" class="ltx_ref"><span class="ltx_text ltx_ref_tag">4</span></a> shows that the performance of nearly all clients exhibits a clear unimodal trend with respect to <math id="A5.p1.m5" class="ltx_Math" alttext="\lambda" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mi>λ</mi><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\lambda</annotation></semantics></math>, with intermediate mixing weights outperforming both extreme settings.
This observation confirms that neither purely general knowledge nor purely personalized knowledge is sufficient, and that an appropriate combination of the two yields superior performance.
Moreover, as the FedIT model is trained for more communication rounds, the peak of the unimodal curves shifts noticeably toward larger <math id="A5.p1.m6" class="ltx_Math" alttext="\lambda" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mi>λ</mi><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\lambda</annotation></semantics></math> for nearly all clients.
Consistently, the mixing weights estimated by our method (indicated by red dashed lines) also move to the right as the FedIT round increases.
This behavior indicates that a better-trained FedIT model contributes more reliable general knowledge to the merged model.
This rightward shift further suggests that the Fisher information associated with the FedIT model increases as training proceeds, which in turn assigns a larger weight to the FedIT model during model merging.</p>
</div>

<section id="A6" class="ltx_appendix">
<h2 class="ltx_title ltx_title_appendix"><span class="ltx_tag ltx_tag_appendix">Appendix F </span>Computation Time</h2>

<div id="A6.p1" class="ltx_para">
<p id="A6.p1.1" class="ltx_p">We report the computation time required to compute the mixing weights on three benchmarks, as well as the training time of the FedIT model and the local model on the same benchmarks.
We randomly sample 30 data samples from the training set of each client.
As shown in Table <a href="#A6.T10" title="Table 10 ‣ Appendix F Computation Time ‣ Communication-Efficient Personalized Adaptation via Federated-Local Model Merging" class="ltx_ref"><span class="ltx_text ltx_ref_tag">10</span></a>, the computation time for mixing weights is modest compared to the overall training cost.
Notably, this procedure is executed only once and does not introduce additional per-round communication or optimization overhead in the federated learning process.</p>
</div>

<section id="A8" class="ltx_appendix">
<h2 class="ltx_title ltx_title_appendix"><span class="ltx_tag ltx_tag_appendix">Appendix H </span>Difference between Fisher Merging and <span id="A8.2" class="ltx_text ltx_font_smallcaps">Potara</span></h2>

<div id="A8.p1" class="ltx_para">
<p id="A8.p1.1" class="ltx_p">Our proposed method <span id="A8.p1.1.1" class="ltx_text ltx_font_smallcaps">Potara</span> differs from Fisher merging in two fundamental aspects.</p>
</div>
<div id="A8.p2" class="ltx_para">
<p id="A8.p2.1" class="ltx_p">First, these two methods operate in different parameter spaces, which leads to vastly different computational costs.
Fisher merging is performed in the full parameter space of the model. When the model size is small (e.g., fewer than hundred million parameters), the computation of the Fisher information matrix is manageable and does not introduce significant overhead. However, for LLMs, whose parameter size typically exceeds one billion, computing the Fisher information for all parameters becomes computationally prohibitive.
In contrast, our method performs merging in the task vector space and computes the Fisher information only for the LoRA parameters, whose dimensionality is several orders of magnitude smaller than that of the full model. As a result, our approach incurs substantially lower computational overhead and remains practical for LLMs.</p>
</div>
<div id="A8.p3" class="ltx_para">
<p id="A8.p3.1" class="ltx_p">Second, Fisher merging assumes independence between the models being merged and ignores their correlation structure.
Specifically, Fisher merging combines models by weighting them according to their individual Fisher information matrices, without considering correlation between models.
In contrast, our method explicitly models the correlation between the federated model and the local model, which allows us to derive a more principled and optimal mixing weight.</p>
</div>
</section>
</article>
</div>

    <h2>Instructions for reporting errors</h2>
    <p>We are continuing to improve HTML versions of papers, and your feedback helps enhance accessibility and mobile
      support. To report errors in the HTML that will help us improve conversion and rendering, choose any of the
      methods listed below:</p>
    <ul>
      <li>Click the "Report Issue" <span class="mobile-only">(<svg role="presentation"
            style="display: inline-block; vertical-align: middle; fill: var(--text-color);" aria-hidden="true"
            height="1em" viewBox="0 0 640 640">
            <path
              d="M224 160C224 107 267 64 320 64C373 64 416 107 416 160L416 163.6C416 179.3 403.3 192 387.6 192L252.5 192C236.8 192 224.1 179.3 224.1 163.6L224.1 160zM569.6 172.8C580.2 186.9 577.3 207 563.2 217.6L465.4 290.9C470.7 299.8 474.7 309.6 477.2 320L576 320C593.7 320 608 334.3 608 352C608 369.7 593.7 384 576 384L480 384L480 416C480 418.6 479.9 421.3 479.8 423.9L563.2 486.4C577.3 497 580.2 517.1 569.6 531.2C559 545.3 538.9 548.2 524.8 537.6L461.7 490.3C438.5 534.5 395.2 566.5 344 574.2L344 344C344 330.7 333.3 320 320 320C306.7 320 296 330.7 296 344L296 574.2C244.8 566.5 201.5 534.5 178.3 490.3L115.2 537.6C101.1 548.2 81 545.3 70.4 531.2C59.8 517.1 62.7 497 76.8 486.4L160.2 423.9C160.1 421.3 160 418.7 160 416L160 384L64 384C46.3 384 32 369.7 32 352C32 334.3 46.3 320 64 320L162.8 320C165.3 309.6 169.3 299.8 174.6 290.9L76.8 217.6C62.7 207 59.8 186.9 70.4 172.8C81 158.7 101.1 155.8 115.2 166.4L224 248C236.3 242.9 249.8 240 264 240L376 240C390.2 240 403.7 242.8 416 248L524.8 166.4C538.9 155.8 559 158.7 569.6 172.8z" />
          </svg>)</span> button, located in the page header.</li>
    </ul>
    <p><strong>Tip:</strong> You can select the relevant text first, to include it in your report.</p>
    <p>Our team has already identified <a class="ltx_ref" href="https://github.com/arXiv/html_feedback/issues"
        target="_blank">the following issues</a>. We appreciate your time reviewing and reporting rendering errors we
      may not have found yet. Your efforts will help us improve the HTML versions for all readers, because disability
      should not be a barrier to accessing research. Thank you for your continued support in championing open access for
      all.</p>
    <p>Have a free development cycle? Help support accessibility at arXiv! Our collaborators at LaTeXML maintain a <a
        class="ltx_ref" href="https://github.com/brucemiller/LaTeXML/wiki/Porting-LaTeX-packages-for-LaTeXML"
        target="_blank">list of packages that need conversion</a>, and welcome <a class="ltx_ref"
        href="https://github.com/brucemiller/LaTeXML/issues" target="_blank">developer contributions</a>.</p>
